Covariance-Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference

Siyuan Chen Affiliation: School of Statistics and Data ScienceShanghai University of Finance and Economics    Yang Bai Affiliation: School of Statistics and Data ScienceShanghai University of Finance and Economics    Huichen Zhu Affiliation: Department of Statistics and Data ScienceThe Chinese University of Hong Kong
Abstract

Covariance-calibrated prediction-powered inference (CC-PPI) uses unlabeled prediction scores to calibrate the covariance weight in a GMM estimator. The raw target preserves the prediction-corrected channel and replaces the labeled prediction-covariance contribution in the auxiliary residual metric with its unlabeled counterpart. Spectral protection ensures positive definiteness, and the estimator uses an equal blend of the original covariance and the protected target. We establish first-order efficiency and derive exact finite-sample risk identities for linear regression, including a design-based improvement theorem with tolerance to prediction error. A quadratic decision model gives a midpoint minimax-regret interpretation of the half-strength default. Exact strength-path formulas and convergent risk approximations bound its distance from the best fixed strength on that path. Simulations and four real-data studies show substantial reductions in parameter MSE. Independent fixed-strength references yield only small further gains on the calibration paths studied.

Keywords: prediction-powered inference; generalized method of moments; covariance calibration; finite-sample inference.

1 Introduction

Prediction-powered inference (PPI) combines a small labeled sample with predictions on a larger unlabeled sample to estimate a population parameter (Angelopoulos et al., 2023). The predictor may be imperfect: a labeled correction removes its population bias when labeled and unlabeled covariates share a distribution. PPI++ tunes a scalar correction (Angelopoulos et al., 2024), PSPA uses coordinate corrections (Miao et al., 2025), and prediction de-correlated inference (PDC) uses a full correction matrix (Gan et al., 2024). Their first-order behavior can be compared through the influence maps generated by a common set of supervised and auxiliary moments.

Estimators with the same first-order correction can differ at finite sample sizes. In a stacked generalized method of moments (GMM) formulation (Hansen, 1982), the criterion is g^​(θ)⊤​W​g^​(θ)\widehat{g}(\theta)^{\top}W\widehat{g}(\theta) with g^=(m1⊤,m2⊤)⊤\widehat{g}=(m_{1}^{\top},m_{2}^{\top})^{\top} and a 2​d×2​d2d\times 2d weight. Its limiting influence map depends on the coefficient W11−1​W12W_{11}^{-1}W_{12}, but its finite-sample stationarity equation also retains the auxiliary sample Jacobian. Minimizing this criterion can therefore give a different estimate from solving a coefficient-corrected equation. Estimated-weight and moment/Jacobian effects are classical sources of finite-sample differences (Newey and Smith, 2004; Windmeijer, 2005).

We formulate a GMM-PPI family by blending the estimated joint covariance with a target and introduce covariance-calibrated PPI (CC-PPI). At a supervised pilot, CC-PPI uses the unlabeled prediction-score covariance to calibrate the auxiliary residual metric while preserving the prediction-corrected channel. We clip the relative covariance update to preserve positive definiteness and use a half-strength blend. Section 3.4 gives the four-step procedure; Section 5.2 derives its raw target from channel preservation and unlabeled covariance calibration.

We study the resulting estimator through its construction, efficiency, finite-sample risk and empirical performance.

  1. (i)

    Covariance calibration. We characterize channel-preserving targets (Proposition 5.1), derive the selected raw target with the unlabeled covariance pool (Proposition 5.2), and establish that spectral protection retains the structure and positive definiteness. The construction requires only the supplied data and predictions.

  2. (ii)

    Efficiency and finite-sample risk. We establish the fixed-moment GMM efficiency bound and conditions under which CC-PPI retains it. In linear regression, an exact signed risk-transfer identity analyzes the complete same-data estimator without Gaussian errors (Theorem 5.3). A primitive design theorem proves strict improvement and quantifies tolerance to prediction error (Theorem 5.4).

  3. (iii)

    Default strength and path-risk comparison. The protected path admits exact realized-loss analysis and convergent population-risk approximations. We derive deterministic and conditional regret bounds, and derive a midpoint minimax-regret interpretation of half strength under quadratic excess risk. Independent reference experiments quantify the small remaining gains along the calibration path.

  4. (iv)

    Simulations and data applications. Linear and logistic simulations show substantial reductions in parameter MSE, with covariance calibration improving the full GMM fit in many configurations. An exact noisy-surrogate example illustrates the efficiency advantage of full correction. Four real-data studies compare the method using externally trained predictors and an independently trained fixed-strength reference.

The construction applies to smooth moments. We develop the exact parameter-risk theory for linear regression and evaluate nonlinear logistic moments empirically. Supplementary Section S5.4 contains the extended numerical diagnostics and implementation details.

Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 defines the family and method; Sections 4 and 5 develop the theory; Sections 6 and 7 report the experiments. Proofs and reproducibility details are in the supplementary material.

2 Related Work

Prediction-powered inference and its variants.

PPI (Angelopoulos et al., 2023) and PPI++ (Angelopoulos et al., 2024) combine labeled and predicted outcomes through a scalar correction; PSPA (Miao et al., 2025) allows a per-coordinate weight; PDC (Gan et al., 2024) uses a full-matrix de-correlation; cross-PPI (Zrnic and Candès, 2024) and task-specific extensions (Miao and Lu, 2024; Motwani and Witten, 2023) broaden the setting. Mozer (2026) observes that the correction is the survey-sampling difference estimator. CC-PPI works with the same correction structure and calibrates the covariance of the stacked moments before inversion.

GMM with auxiliary data and estimated weights.

Efficient two-sample GMM and its semiparametric efficiency are classical (Hansen, 1982; Newey and McFadden, 1994; Chen et al., 2008); combining samples of unequal length or with missing data is treated in (Lynch and Wachter, 2013; Chaudhuri and Guilkey, 2016; Muris, 2010; Franguridi and Moon, 2025). The finite-sample cost of estimated weights is well documented (Altonji and Segal, 1996; Windmeijer, 2005; Newey and Smith, 2004; Hwang and Sun, 2018). Our finite-sample risk analysis keeps the joint dependence of the pilot, moments and estimated weight.

Finite-sample shrinkage and tuning.

Normal-mean shrinkage separates direction from magnitude (Tan, 2015); aggregation of affine estimators and of ordered smoothers shows tuning can be nearly cost-free (Bellec, 2018; Bellec and Yang, 2020); Stein’s unbiased risk estimate and its optimism are studied in (Bellec and Zhang, 2021; Tibshirani and Rosset, 2019; Cauchois et al., 2021). Efficient shrinkage in parametric GMM and the risk of averaging estimators are treated in (Hansen, 2016; Cheng et al., 2019). For CC-PPI, we derive a conditional scalar optimum under the stated sign assumptions and a midpoint minimax-regret rule under quadratic excess risk. The full strength path is generally rational, so its risk requires a separate analysis.

Surrogate, imputation, and synthetic data.

Prediction- and surrogate-powered inference (Chen et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2026), synthetic-data inference (Byun et al., 2025), and imputation-powered inference (Duan and Pelger, 2025; Zhao and Candès, 2025) all replace a missing or expensive quantity by a predicted one. The non-asymptotic limits of PPI are analyzed in (Mani et al., 2025). CC-PPI studies how covariance regularization affects the finite-sample risk of the corrected estimator. The prediction function may be misspecified.

3 Problem Setup and the GMM-PPI Family

Members of the GMM-PPI family use the same labeled data, unlabeled covariates and prediction function, but regularize the joint moment covariance differently before inversion. We define the moments and covariance weights below, then specify CC-PPI in four steps in Section 3.4.

3.1 Data, target, and prediction-assisted moments

Let (X,Y)∼ℙ(X,Y)\sim\mathbb{P}. We observe a labeled sample ℒ={(Xi,Yi)}i=1n\mathcal{L}=\{(X_{i},Y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} and an independent unlabeled sample 𝒰={X~j}j=1N\mathcal{U}=\{\widetilde{X}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}. Each sample is independently and identically distributed, and both covariate samples follow the same marginal distribution. We have access to a prediction function ff constructed independently of both inference samples. In typical applications, ff is supplied as a black box: only its predictions are required, with no access to its internal structure or training procedure. We condition on ff throughout the analysis.

The target θ∗∈Θ⊆ℝd\theta_{*}\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} is the unique solution of

𝔼⁡{ψ⁡(X,Y,θ∗)}=0,\mathbb{E}\{\psi(X,Y;\theta_{*})\}=0, (1)

where ψ\psi is a known dd-dimensional estimating function. For differentiable loss minimization, ψ⁡(x,y,θ)=∇θℓθ​(x,y)\psi(x,y;\theta)=\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{\theta}(x,y), with θ∗\theta_{*} an interior population minimizer. Estimating equations without an underlying loss are also permitted.

Let h⁡(x,θ)h(x;\theta) be a dd-dimensional auxiliary function computable from xx and f⁡(x)f(x). Our main choice is

h⁡(x,θ)=ψ⁡(x,f⁡(x),θ).h(x;\theta)=\psi(x,f(x);\theta). (2)

This substitution is appropriate when the estimating function is defined for the prediction output. More generally, a specified transformation of xx and f⁡(x)f(x) can be used. Once chosen, the same auxiliary function is used throughout the family. Define

m1​(θ)\displaystyle m_{1}(\theta) =1n​∑i=1nψ⁡(Xi,Yi,θ),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi(X_{i},Y_{i};\theta), (3)
m2​(θ)\displaystyle m_{2}(\theta) =1N​∑j=1Nh⁡(X~j,θ)−1n​∑i=1nh⁡(Xi,θ),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}h(\widetilde{X}_{j};\theta)-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}h(X_{i};\theta), (4)
g^​(θ)\displaystyle\widehat{g}(\theta) =(m1​(θ)⊤,m2​(θ)⊤)⊤.\displaystyle=\bigl(m_{1}(\theta)^{\top},m_{2}(\theta)^{\top}\bigr)^{\top}. (5)

For every fixed θ\theta at which the expectations exist,

𝔼​{m2​(θ)}=0.\mathbb{E}\{m_{2}(\theta)\}=0. (6)

Prediction misspecification therefore does not change the population identifying equation. The auxiliary moment supplies information through its dependence with the supervised moment. The sampling, integrability and regularity conditions stated below still apply. The difference of auxiliary means is the prediction-based correction familiar from PPI (Angelopoulos et al., 2023); here the two moment vectors are retained separately in a joint quadratic criterion.

3.2 Joint moment covariance

Set M=min⁡(n,N)M=\min(n,N), c1,n=M/nc_{1,n}=M/n, and c2,n=M/Nc_{2,n}=M/N. At θ∗\theta_{*}, write

Σ11=Var⁡(ψ),Σ1​h=Cov⁡(ψ,h),Σh​h=Var⁡(h),\Sigma_{11}=\operatorname{Var}(\psi),\quad\Sigma_{1h}=\operatorname{Cov}(\psi,h),\quad\Sigma_{hh}=\operatorname{Var}(h), (7)

with arguments suppressed. Independence gives

Var⁡{M​g^​(θ∗)}=Sn=(c1,n​Σ11−c1,n​Σ1​h−c1,n​Σ1​h⊤(c1,n+c2,n)​Σh​h).\operatorname{Var}\{\sqrt{M}\,\widehat{g}(\theta_{*})\}=S_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}c_{1,n}\Sigma_{11}&-c_{1,n}\Sigma_{1h}\\ -c_{1,n}\Sigma_{1h}^{\top}&(c_{1,n}+c_{2,n})\Sigma_{hh}\end{pmatrix}. (8)

The negative cross block follows from the sign of the labeled auxiliary mean. Under a stable sample-size ratio, SnS_{n} has a limit SS. Positive definiteness of this limit is a condition for the regular efficiency analysis, not a restriction on every local sequence studied later.

Obtain a supervised initial estimate tt, typically by solving m1​(t)=0m_{1}(t)=0, and evaluate

si=ψ⁡(Xi,Yi,t),hi=h⁡(Xi,t),hjU=h⁡(X~j,t).s_{i}=\psi(X_{i},Y_{i};t),\quad h_{i}=h(X_{i};t),\quad h_{j}^{U}=h(\widetilde{X}_{j};t). (9)

For a sample of size kk, use the centered covariance

Cov^k​(a,b)=1k​∑i=1k(ai−a¯)​(bi−b¯)⊤.\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{k}(a,b)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}(a_{i}-\bar{a})(b_{i}-\bar{b})^{\top}. (10)

If m1​(t)=0m_{1}(t)=0 exactly, centering supervised scores changes neither their covariance nor the cross covariance with auxiliary scores. With a numerical regularizer εM≥0\varepsilon_{M}\geq 0, define

V^\displaystyle\widehat{V} =c1,n​Cov^ℒ​(s,s)+εM​Id,\displaystyle=c_{1,n}\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{L}}(s,s)+\varepsilon_{M}I_{d}, (11)
R^\displaystyle\widehat{R} =c1,n​Cov^ℒ​(s,h),\displaystyle=c_{1,n}\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{L}}(s,h), (12)
D^\displaystyle\widehat{D} =c1,n​Cov^ℒ​(h,h)+c2,n​Cov^𝒰​(hU,hU)+εM​Id,\displaystyle=c_{1,n}\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{L}}(h,h)+c_{2,n}\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{U}}(h^{U},h^{U})+\varepsilon_{M}I_{d}, (13)
S^\displaystyle\widehat{S} =(V^−R^−R^⊤D^).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat{V}&-\widehat{R}\\ -\widehat{R}^{\top}&\widehat{D}\end{pmatrix}. (14)

Before regularization, this is a scaled labeled covariance of (si⊤,−hi⊤)⊤(s_{i}^{\top},-h_{i}^{\top})^{\top} plus a positive semidefinite unlabeled contribution. It is therefore positive semidefinite; εM>0\varepsilon_{M}>0 makes it positive definite. The ridge value is part of the estimator specification. Retaining the unregularized covariance limit requires εM→0\varepsilon_{M}\to 0.

3.3 A family of covariance-weighted estimators

Let S0,n​(α)S_{0,n}(\alpha) be a symmetric positive definite target, where α\alpha indexes a specified target collection. Targets may depend on the data, initial estimate, and sample sizes. For 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq 1, set

S^λ,α\displaystyle\widehat{S}_{\lambda,\alpha} =(1−λ)​S^+λ​S0,n​(α),\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)\widehat{S}+\lambda S_{0,n}(\alpha), (15)
Wλ,α\displaystyle W_{\lambda,\alpha} =S^λ,α−1,\displaystyle=\widehat{S}_{\lambda,\alpha}^{-1}, (16)
Qn​(θ,λ,α)\displaystyle Q_{n}(\theta;\lambda,\alpha) =g^​(θ)⊤​Wλ,α​g^​(θ),\displaystyle=\widehat{g}(\theta)^{\top}W_{\lambda,\alpha}\widehat{g}(\theta), (17)
θ^λ,α\displaystyle\widehat{\theta}_{\lambda,\alpha} ∈arg​minθ∈Θ⁡Qn​(θ,λ,α).\displaystyle\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\in\Theta}Q_{n}(\theta;\lambda,\alpha). (18)

If S^≻0\widehat{S}\succ 0, the blend is positive definite for all λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]. If the unregularized S^\widehat{S} is singular, a positive definite target gives an invertible blend for λ>0\lambda>0; the endpoint λ=0\lambda=0 requires separate treatment.

Both tuning quantities may be data dependent. After selection, tt, S^\widehat{S}, the target, and the tuning quantities are held fixed during minimization. Recomputing the weight at each candidate θ\theta defines a different criterion with additional derivative terms.

The target specifies which covariance features are regularized, and λ\lambda sets the strength. The finite-sample analysis studies the risk of these choices.

The 2​d×2​d2d\times 2d matrix Wλ,αW_{\lambda,\alpha} weights the stacked moments; the d×dd\times d matrix Λ\Lambda in m1+Λ​m2=0m_{1}+\Lambda m_{2}=0 is a correction coefficient. The relation between them is derived in the next section.

CC-PPI supplies the concrete covariance target developed below. Cross-block, spherical and diagonal alternatives, together with a sample-size benchmark strength, are specified in Supplementary Section S1.1 as additional members of the GMM-PPI family.

3.4 Covariance-calibrated PPI: construction and estimation

Covariance-calibrated PPI (CC-PPI) chooses a target using the unlabeled prediction scores. Given m1m_{1} and m2m_{2}, the following four steps define the estimator. Section 5 analyzes its risk.

  1. 1.

    Obtain the pilot and evaluate the scores. Compute a supervised estimate tt by solving m1​(t)=0m_{1}(t)=0, or by the specified supervised fitting procedure. Evaluate si=ψ⁡(Xi,Yi,t)s_{i}=\psi(X_{i},Y_{i};t), hi=h⁡(Xi,t)h_{i}=h(X_{i};t) and hjU=h⁡(X~j,t)h_{j}^{U}=h(\widetilde{X}_{j};t) as in (9). Here h⁡(x,θ)=ψ⁡(x,f⁡(x),θ)h(x;\theta)=\psi(x,f(x);\theta) is a vector of prediction-based scores, not the prediction itself. For squared-loss linear regression, for example, si=Xi​(Xi⊤​t−Yi)s_{i}=X_{i}(X_{i}^{\top}t-Y_{i}) and hi=Xi​(Xi⊤​t−f⁡(Xi))h_{i}=X_{i}(X_{i}^{\top}t-f(X_{i})), with the same substitution on the unlabeled sample. All quantities used to construct the weight are evaluated at this pilot.

  2. 2.

    Estimate the joint moment covariance. Use the centered sample covariance with divisor equal to sample size in (10). Define

    CL=Cov^ℒ​(h,h),CU=Cov^𝒰​(hU,hU).C_{L}=\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{L}}(h,h),\qquad C_{U}=\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{U}}(h^{U},h^{U}). (19)

    These are covariances of the dd-dimensional prediction scores at tt. Form S^\widehat{S} using (11)–(14), with εM>0\varepsilon_{M}>0. To keep the calibration on one scale, put ρ=n/N\rho=n/N, η=εM/c1,n\eta=\varepsilon_{M}/c_{1,n} and 𝖲=S^/c1,n\mathsf{S}=\widehat{S}/c_{1,n}, so that

    𝖲=(Cov^ℒ​(s,s)+η​Id−Cov^ℒ​(s,h)−Cov^ℒ​(s,h)⊤CL+ρ​CU+η​Id).\mathsf{S}=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{L}}(s,s)+\eta I_{d}&-\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{L}}(s,h)\\ -\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{L}}(s,h)^{\top}&C_{L}+\rho C_{U}+\eta I_{d}\end{pmatrix}. (20)

    Thus 𝖲\mathsf{S} is the estimated covariance on the nn scale; multiplying the whole covariance by c1,n>0c_{1,n}>0 does not change the GMM minimizer. The experiments use N≥nN\geq n and η=n−2\eta=n^{-2}, for which c1,n=1c_{1,n}=1.

  3. 3.

    Calibrate and protect the covariance. The full GMM criterion contains an auxiliary residual penalty in addition to the prediction-corrected component. We use the unlabeled prediction-score covariance to calibrate the metric of this penalty while preserving the covariance structure of the prediction-corrected channel; Section 5 develops the finite-sample rationale. The raw difference and its joint-moment update are

    K=CU−CL,T=(Id−Id),Δ=T​K​T⊤=(K−K−KK).K=C_{U}-C_{L},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}I_{d}\\ -I_{d}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Delta=TKT^{\top}=\begin{pmatrix}K&-K\\ -K&K\end{pmatrix}. (21)

    In the basis (c,m2)(c,m_{2}), where c=m1+m2c=m_{1}+m_{2} is the prediction-corrected moment, let Bc=(IdId0Id)B_{c}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I_{d}&I_{d}\\ 0&I_{d}\end{smallmatrix}\right). Then Bc​Δ​Bc⊤=diag⁡(0,K)B_{c}\Delta B_{c}^{\top}=\operatorname{diag}(0,K): the covariance of cc and its cross covariance with m2m_{2} are preserved, while the auxiliary covariance changes from CL+ρ​CU+η​IdC_{L}+\rho C_{U}+\eta I_{d} to (1+ρ)​CU+η​Id(1+\rho)C_{U}+\eta I_{d}. The update therefore replaces the labeled prediction-covariance contribution with its unlabeled counterpart while preserving the corrected channel.

    Under common covariate sampling, CLC_{L} and CUC_{U} estimate the same population score covariance in the regular limit. A large unlabeled sample supplies additional information about that covariance. This motivates the calibration, but does not imply that CUC_{U} is always more accurate at the fitted pilot or that the raw update always lowers parameter risk.

    The raw update may be too large to preserve positive definiteness. Protect it by whitening with 𝖲\mathsf{S}, clipping eigenvalues, and returning to the original scale:

    E\displaystyle E =𝖲−1/2Δ𝖲−1/2=Qdiag(e1,…,e2​d)Q⊤,\displaystyle=\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}\Delta\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}=Q\operatorname{diag}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{2d})Q^{\top},
    e~k\displaystyle\widetilde{e}_{k} =max⁡{−κ,min⁡(ek,κ)},Ep=Q​diag⁡(e~1,…,e~2​d)​Q⊤,\displaystyle=\max\{-\kappa,\min(e_{k},\kappa)\},\qquad E_{p}=Q\operatorname{diag}(\widetilde{e}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{e}_{2d})Q^{\top},
    Δp\displaystyle\Delta_{p} =𝖲1/2​Ep​𝖲1/2,κ=1/2.\displaystyle=\mathsf{S}^{1/2}E_{p}\mathsf{S}^{1/2},\qquad\kappa=1/2. (22)

    All square roots are symmetric positive definite matrix square roots. Clipping acts on eigenvalues, not individual matrix entries. It bounds the change relative to the current covariance, giving (1−λ​κ)​𝖲⪯𝖲+λ​Δp⪯(1+λ​κ)​𝖲(1-\lambda\kappa)\mathsf{S}\preceq\mathsf{S}+\lambda\Delta_{p}\preceq(1+\lambda\kappa)\mathsf{S} for 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq 1.

  4. 4.

    Blend at half strength and fit with the frozen weight. The protected covariance target and its blend, expressed on the original MM scale, are

    S0,ncal=c1,n​(𝖲+Δp),S^λ=(1−λ)​S^+λ​S0,ncal=c1,n​(𝖲+λ​Δp).S_{0,n}^{\rm cal}=c_{1,n}(\mathsf{S}+\Delta_{p}),\qquad\widehat{S}_{\lambda}=(1-\lambda)\widehat{S}+\lambda S_{0,n}^{\rm cal}=c_{1,n}(\mathsf{S}+\lambda\Delta_{p}). (23)

    CC-PPI uses the fixed default

    λCC=1/2,\lambda_{\rm CC}=1/2, (24)

    and estimates the parameter by

    θ^CC∈arg​minθ∈Θ⁡g^​(θ)⊤​S^λCC−1​g^​(θ).\widehat{\theta}_{\rm CC}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\in\Theta}\widehat{g}(\theta)^{\top}\widehat{S}_{\lambda_{\rm CC}}^{-1}\widehat{g}(\theta). (25)

    The pilot, covariances and protected update remain fixed throughout optimization; only the moments vary with θ\theta. Section 3.5 gives the closed-form solution for affine moments and the optimization requirements for nonlinear moments. The cap κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 controls the largest relative perturbation, whereas λCC=1/2\lambda_{\rm CC}=1/2 blends the original covariance and the protected target equally; these are distinct choices. Their combination puts the relative covariance eigenvalues in [3/4,5/4][3/4,5/4]. Half strength is a default, not a universally optimal tuning parameter. Section 5 uses hh to denote this fixed strength, separately from the auxiliary function h⁡(x,θ)h(x;\theta).

An equivalent implementation of Step 3 requires a d×dd\times d spectral decomposition. Define

F=T⊤​𝖲−1​T,F=T^{\top}\mathsf{S}^{-1}T, (26)

and apply the same eigenvalue clipping to obtain

Kp=F−1/2clip[−κ,κ](F1/2(CU−CL)F1/2)F−1/2,Δp=TKpT⊤.K_{p}=F^{-1/2}\operatorname{clip}_{[-\kappa,\kappa]}\bigl(F^{1/2}(C_{U}-C_{L})F^{1/2}\bigr)F^{-1/2},\qquad\Delta_{p}=TK_{p}T^{\top}. (27)

This equals (22) because 𝖲−1/2TF−1/2\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}TF^{-1/2} has orthonormal columns and clipping maps zero to zero. In particular, protection retains the channel-preserving structure of the raw update.

The calibration of S^λCC\widehat{S}_{\lambda_{\rm CC}} is designed for GMM parameter estimation; minimizing covariance-estimation error is a different objective. Section 5.2 formalizes the two principles defining the raw target. With the pool fixed to CUC_{U}, they determine the raw target, and spectral protection completes the method specification. Under the regular conditions of Section 4, CU−CL→p0C_{U}-C_{L}\to_{p}0, so the calibration vanishes and CC-PPI retains first-order efficiency. Section 5 studies its finite-sample parameter risk, which depends on the design and predictor.

3.5 Frozen-weight optimization and implementation

For differentiable moments, write

A1​(θ)=∂m1​(θ)∂θ⊤,A5​(θ)=∂m2​(θ)∂θ⊤,J^​(θ)=(A1​(θ)A5​(θ)).A_{1}(\theta)=\frac{\partial m_{1}(\theta)}{\partial\theta^{\top}},\quad A_{5}(\theta)=\frac{\partial m_{2}(\theta)}{\partial\theta^{\top}},\quad\widehat{J}(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}A_{1}(\theta)\\ A_{5}(\theta)\end{pmatrix}. (28)

An interior minimizer satisfies

J^​(θ^)⊤​Wλ,α​g^​(θ^)=0.\widehat{J}(\widehat{\theta})^{\top}W_{\lambda,\alpha}\widehat{g}(\widehat{\theta})=0. (29)

Although the auxiliary population moment is identically zero, its sample derivative A5A_{5} need not vanish. The criterion retains the sample moment path; its risk consequences and anchor interpretation are studied in the finite-sample section.

For affine moments g^​(θ)=H​θ−b\widehat{g}(\theta)=H\theta-b, with HH of full column rank, the unconstrained solution is

θ^λ,α=(H⊤​Wλ,α​H)−1​H⊤​Wλ,α​b.\widehat{\theta}_{\lambda,\alpha}=(H^{\top}W_{\lambda,\alpha}H)^{-1}H^{\top}W_{\lambda,\alpha}b. (30)

For nonlinear moments, the criterion need not be convex. Implementations must specify initialization and stopping rules, and check objective values and first-order residuals. A stationary point alone does not certify a global minimum.

Supplementary Section S1.2 gives an optional one-step approximation and its first-order equivalence to the full fit. For nonlinear moments, the approximation and the frozen-criterion minimizer can differ at finite sample sizes.

Relative to inverse-covariance GMM with the same moments and pilot tt, the additional computation after forming S^\widehat{S} is target construction and strength selection. The displayed targets and benchmark strength require no additional labels, true parameters, or access to the internals of ff. A learned auxiliary function or a separate pilot split defines a different procedure.

3.6 Scope of the construction

GMM determines how the joint moments enter the quadratic criterion (Hansen, 1982). First-order efficiency depends on the limiting weight, while finite-sample parameter risk also depends on weight estimation and optimization. We analyze these two questions in turn.

The next section gives the regular efficiency bound and the conditions under which weight perturbations preserve it. The finite-sample analysis then examines the correction and auxiliary penalty, including the randomness of estimated weights and selected strengths. Degenerating auxiliary covariances fall outside the fixed positive definite limit used for the regular theory.

A qq-dimensional auxiliary function is also permitted: the stacked vector has dimension d+qd+q, the cross block is d×qd\times q, and each spherical block uses its own dimension. Efficiency comparisons must keep the chosen auxiliary information fixed.

PPI++ and PSPA provide related approaches to prediction-assisted adaptation (Angelopoulos et al., 2024; Miao et al., 2025). Supplementary Section S5 describes their relation to this construction. Supplementary Sections S1 and S2 contain the probability and matrix-algebra arguments.

4 First-Order Efficiency and Optimal Weighting

For the moments in Section 3, we compare limiting parameter covariances in the Loewner order, conditional on the externally constructed predictor ff. The classical GMM bound (Hansen, 1982) identifies which family members are first-order efficient. The comparison holds the auxiliary information fixed and concerns parameter covariances, rather than an ordering of the weight matrices.

4.1 Regularity and the joint moment limit

Throughout this section, dd and ff are fixed, n,N→∞n,N\to\infty, and n/N→r∈[0,∞)n/N\to r\in[0,\infty). With the normalization of Section 3.2, write c1=limM/n>0c_{1}=\lim M/n>0 and c2=limM/N≥0c_{2}=\lim M/N\geq 0. Thus c2/c1=rc_{2}/c_{1}=r. All expectations and probability limits below are conditional on ff when it is random. Define

μ⁡(θ)=𝔼⁡{ψ⁡(X,Y,θ)},g⁡(θ)=(μ⁡(θ)0),A=∂μ⁡(θ)∂θ⊤|θ=θ∗,G=(A0).\mu(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\{\psi(X,Y;\theta)\},\qquad g(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\mu(\theta)\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=\left.\frac{\partial\mu(\theta)}{\partial\theta^{\top}}\right|_{\theta=\theta_{*}},\qquad G=\begin{pmatrix}A\\ 0\end{pmatrix}. (31)

The zero lower block follows from the identical covariate distributions; it is not a statement that the sample derivative A5A_{5} vanishes.

We use the following regular conditions.

  1. (R1)

    Θ\Theta is compact, θ∗\theta_{*} is an interior point, and μ\mu is continuous with unique zero θ∗\theta_{*}. The uniform law supθ∈Θ‖g^​(θ)−g⁡(θ)‖​→𝑝​0\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|\widehat{g}(\theta)-g(\theta)\|\overset{p}{\to}0 holds. Compactness may be replaced by another condition that yields consistency of the selected minimizer.

  2. (R2)

    On an open neighborhood of θ∗\theta_{*}, the sample moments are continuously differentiable and their Jacobians converge uniformly in probability to the continuous population Jacobian. Differentiation under expectation is valid, and AA is nonsingular.

  3. (R3)

    ψ⁡(X,Y,θ∗)\psi(X,Y;\theta_{*}) and h⁡(X,θ∗)h(X;\theta_{*}) have finite second moments. Their joint covariance gives

    S=(V−R−R⊤D)≻0,V=c1​Σ11,R=c1​Σ1​h,D=(c1+c2)​Σh​h.S=\begin{pmatrix}V&-R\\ -R^{\top}&D\end{pmatrix}\succ 0,\qquad V=c_{1}\Sigma_{11},\quad R=c_{1}\Sigma_{1h},\quad D=(c_{1}+c_{2})\Sigma_{hh}. (32)
  4. (R4)

    The frozen weight satisfies Wn​→𝑝​W≻0W_{n}\overset{p}{\to}W\succ 0. The estimator is a measurable global minimizer of its frozen criterion. A numerical approximation is also allowed if it satisfies Qn​(θ^)≤infΘQn+op​(1)Q_{n}(\widehat{\theta})\leq\inf_{\Theta}Q_{n}+o_{p}(1) and J^(θ^)⊤Wng^(θ^)=op(M−1/2)\widehat{J}(\widehat{\theta})^{\top}W_{n}\widehat{g}(\widehat{\theta})=o_{p}(M^{-1/2}).

These fixed-dimension conditions require a positive definite limiting moment covariance. Sequences with singular limits need a different analysis.

Under (R3), the independent-sample central limit theorem gives

M​g^​(θ∗)⇒N⁡(0,S).\sqrt{M}\,\widehat{g}(\theta_{*})\Rightarrow N(0,S). (33)

Indeed, the labeled contribution is the centered average of (ψ⊤,−h⊤)⊤(\psi^{\top},-h^{\top})^{\top}, and the unlabeled contribution is the centered average of (0⊤,h⊤)⊤(0^{\top},h^{\top})^{\top}. Their variances add to (32). If c2=0c_{2}=0, the unlabeled fluctuation vanishes in probability by its second moment bound.

The consistency of the covariance estimator requires a further condition when it is evaluated at the random pilot tt. We assume t​→𝑝​θ∗t\overset{p}{\to}\theta_{*}, uniform laws for the score first and second products near θ∗\theta_{*}, continuity of their expectations, and εM→0\varepsilon_{M}\to 0. These imply S^​→𝑝​S\widehat{S}\overset{p}{\to}S. A sufficient route is continuity of the scores together with square-integrable local envelopes for ψ\psi and hh. This covariance condition is imposed wherever the feasible inverse-covariance weight or a plug-in covariance is used.

4.2 Asymptotic distribution for a general weight

Theorem 4.1 (General frozen weight).

Under (R1)–(R4), the estimator is consistent and

M​(θ^−θ∗)\displaystyle\sqrt{M}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{*}) =−K⁡(W)​M​g^​(θ∗)+op​(1),\displaystyle=-K(W)\sqrt{M}\,\widehat{g}(\theta_{*})+o_{p}(1), (34)
K⁡(W)\displaystyle K(W) =(G⊤​W​G)−1​G⊤​W,\displaystyle=(G^{\top}WG)^{-1}G^{\top}W, (35)
M​(θ^−θ∗)\displaystyle\sqrt{M}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{*}) ⇒N​{0,𝒱⁡(W)},\displaystyle\Rightarrow N\{0,\mathcal{V}(W)\}, (36)
𝒱⁡(W)\displaystyle\mathcal{V}(W) =K⁡(W)​S​K​(W)⊤.\displaystyle=K(W)SK(W)^{\top}. (37)

The weight may be estimated from the same inference samples; independence between WnW_{n} and the moments is not required.

Proof.

The frozen criterion converges uniformly to g​(θ)⊤​W​g​(θ)g(\theta)^{\top}Wg(\theta). Positive definiteness of WW and (R1) give its unique minimizer θ∗\theta_{*}, hence consistency. Uniform Jacobian convergence and a Taylor expansion around θ∗\theta_{*} give

0=G⊤Wg^(θ∗)+{G⊤WG+op(1)}(θ^−θ∗)+op(M−1/2).0=G^{\top}W\widehat{g}(\theta_{*})+\{G^{\top}WG+o_{p}(1)\}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{*})+o_{p}(M^{-1/2}). (38)

Here the coefficient of g^​(θ∗)\widehat{g}(\theta_{*}) differs from G⊤​WG^{\top}W by op​(1)o_{p}(1), whose product with the Op(M−1/2)O_{p}(M^{-1/2}) moment is negligible. Nonsingularity of G⊤​W​GG^{\top}WG gives (34). The central limit theorem and Slutsky’s theorem complete the proof. The argument uses convergence in probability of the estimated weight, not independence from the moments. ∎

4.3 Loewner optimality and equality conditions

Theorem 4.2 (Optimal parameter covariance).

For S≻0S\succ 0 and GG of full column rank, define

K∗=(G⊤​S−1​G)−1​G⊤​S−1,𝒱∗=(G⊤​S−1​G)−1.K_{*}=(G^{\top}S^{-1}G)^{-1}G^{\top}S^{-1},\qquad\mathcal{V}_{*}=(G^{\top}S^{-1}G)^{-1}. (39)

For every symmetric positive definite WW,

𝒱⁡(W)−𝒱∗={K⁡(W)−K∗}​S​{K⁡(W)−K∗}⊤⪰0.\mathcal{V}(W)-\mathcal{V}_{*}=\{K(W)-K_{*}\}S\{K(W)-K_{*}\}^{\top}\succeq 0. (40)

Equality of the covariance matrices holds if and only if K⁡(W)=K∗K(W)=K_{*}. For a specified contrast a⊤​θa^{\top}\theta, equality of asymptotic variances holds if and only if a⊤​{K⁡(W)−K∗}=0a^{\top}\{K(W)-K_{*}\}=0.

Proof.

Both K⁡(W)​GK(W)G and K∗​GK_{*}G equal IdI_{d}. Moreover, K∗​S=𝒱∗​G⊤K_{*}S=\mathcal{V}_{*}G^{\top}. Consequently, (K⁡(W)−K∗)​S​K∗⊤=0(K(W)-K_{*})SK_{*}^{\top}=0. Expanding K⁡(W)​S​K​(W)⊤K(W)SK(W)^{\top} gives (40). Positive definiteness of SS yields the matrix and contrast equality conditions. ∎

The unrestricted matrix class attains the bound. Scalar and diagonal restrictions can attain it only when their influence maps agree with the unrestricted optimum. Otherwise the covariance gap is positive semidefinite, though it may vanish for some contrasts. Several weight matrices can therefore attain the same bound.

For the PPI moment structure, the comparison has a more explicit form. Partition a general weight as W=(Wa​b)a,b=12W=(W_{ab})_{a,b=1}^{2} and set

L⁡(W)=W11−1​W12,L∗=R​D−1,C=V−R​D−1​R⊤.L(W)=W_{11}^{-1}W_{12},\qquad L_{*}=RD^{-1},\qquad C=V-RD^{-1}R^{\top}. (41)

Since G=(A⊤,0⊤)⊤G=(A^{\top},0^{\top})^{\top}, direct multiplication gives

K⁡(W)\displaystyle K(W) =A−1​(IdL⁡(W)),\displaystyle=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}I_{d}&L(W)\end{pmatrix}, (42)
𝒱∗\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{*} =A−1​C​A−⁣⊤,\displaystyle=A^{-1}CA^{-\top}, (43)
𝒱⁡(W)−𝒱∗\displaystyle\mathcal{V}(W)-\mathcal{V}_{*} =A−1​{L⁡(W)−L∗}​D​{L⁡(W)−L∗}⊤​A−⁣⊤.\displaystyle=A^{-1}\{L(W)-L_{*}\}D\{L(W)-L_{*}\}^{\top}A^{-\top}. (44)

Here A−⁣⊤=(A−1)⊤A^{-\top}=(A^{-1})^{\top}. Thus first-order efficiency depends on the limiting correction coefficient, even though the finite-sample criterion depends on the entire weight.

A scalar or diagonal stacked GMM weight has W12=0W_{12}=0 and hence L⁡(W)=0L(W)=0, giving the supervised first-order covariance. A scalar or diagonal correction coefficient instead restricts LL to ℓ​Id\ell I_{d} or to a diagonal matrix. For any such coefficient LL, the asymptotic covariance of a regular estimator with influence map A−1​(Id,L)A^{-1}(I_{d},L) obeys (44). The full correction attains equality; a restricted correction does so exactly when it can represent R​D−1RD^{-1}. The auxiliary information is held fixed throughout this comparison.

The nonuniqueness is explicit. For any P,T≻0P,T\succ 0, the matrix

W⁡(P,T)=(PP​L∗L∗⊤​PL∗⊤​P​L∗+T)≻0W(P,T)=\begin{pmatrix}P&PL_{*}\\ L_{*}^{\top}P&L_{*}^{\top}PL_{*}+T\end{pmatrix}\succ 0 (45)

has L⁡(W)=L∗L(W)=L_{*} and attains 𝒱∗\mathcal{V}_{*}. Its Schur complement is TT. Different choices may give different finite-sample criteria, without changing first-order efficiency. Equation (45) describes efficient limiting weights in the general GMM class; it does not assert that every such weight belongs to a prespecified collection of shrinkage targets in Section 3.3.

4.4 Efficiency-preserving covariance weights

Corollary 4.3 (A common inverse-covariance limit).

Suppose the covariance consistency condition holds and the selected family member satisfies

Δn=λn​{S0,n​(αn)−S^}​⟶𝑝​0.\Delta_{n}=\lambda_{n}\{S_{0,n}(\alpha_{n})-\widehat{S}\}\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}0. (46)

Then S^λn,αn​→𝑝​S\widehat{S}_{\lambda_{n},\alpha_{n}}\overset{p}{\to}S and Wλn,αn​→𝑝​S−1W_{\lambda_{n},\alpha_{n}}\overset{p}{\to}S^{-1}. Under the remaining regular conditions, its limiting parameter covariance is 𝒱∗\mathcal{V}_{*}. Any two such estimators computed from the same data satisfy

M​{θ^(a)−θ^(b)}=op​(1).\sqrt{M}\{\widehat{\theta}^{(a)}-\widehat{\theta}^{(b)}\}=o_{p}(1). (47)
Proof.

The blended covariance is S^+Δn\widehat{S}+\Delta_{n}. Continuity of inversion at S≻0S\succ 0 gives the weight limit. Theorem 4.1 gives the common influence map K∗K_{*}. Subtracting the two expansions proves (47). ∎

Condition (46) is satisfied if λn​→𝑝​0\lambda_{n}\overset{p}{\to}0 and the selected target is Op​(1)O_{p}(1). Boundedness must hold for the selected target when its index is data dependent. No independence of the tuning quantities is needed. Alternatively, if S0,n​(αn)​→𝑝​SS_{0,n}(\alpha_{n})\overset{p}{\to}S, every λn∈[0,1]\lambda_{n}\in[0,1] satisfies the condition, even when λn\lambda_{n} does not converge to zero. If the target diverges, vanishing λn\lambda_{n} alone is insufficient.

For the cross-block, spherical, and diagonal targets in Supplementary Section S1.1, covariance consistency implies Op​(1)O_{p}(1) targets. At fixed dd, the benchmark λn=min⁡{0.8,d/n}\lambda_{n}=\min\{0.8,d/n\} therefore preserves S−1S^{-1} and 𝒱∗\mathcal{V}_{*}, provided εM→0\varepsilon_{M}\to 0. This is an efficiency-preservation result, not a finite-sample optimality result. A dimension that increases with nn, or a fixed nonvanishing numerical ridge, requires a different limit analysis.

Sharing S−1S^{-1} is sufficient but not necessary for sharing the efficiency bound. If Wn​→𝑝​W¯≻0W_{n}\overset{p}{\to}\overline{W}\succ 0, equations (42)–(44) show that efficiency is preserved precisely when

W¯11−1​W¯12=R​D−1.\overline{W}_{11}^{-1}\overline{W}_{12}=RD^{-1}. (48)

As a concrete distinction, if the cross-block target is used and λn​→𝑝​λ0\lambda_{n}\overset{p}{\to}\lambda_{0}, then the limiting covariance has cross block −(1−λ0)​R-(1-\lambda_{0})R. Its inverse satisfies L⁡(W¯)=(1−λ0)​R​D−1L(\overline{W})=(1-\lambda_{0})RD^{-1}, so

𝒱⁡(W¯)−𝒱∗=λ02​A−1​R​D−1​R⊤​A−⁣⊤.\mathcal{V}(\overline{W})-\mathcal{V}_{*}=\lambda_{0}^{2}A^{-1}RD^{-1}R^{\top}A^{-\top}. (49)

Thus a nonvanishing cross-block shrinkage loses first-order efficiency when R≠0R\neq 0, although some contrasts may retain equality. If R=0R=0, it preserves the bound. For other target collections, the equality test is (48), rather than a universal requirement that λn→0\lambda_{n}\to 0.

4.5 Feasible inference

Under the covariance consistency condition, let G^=J^​(t)\widehat{G}=\widehat{J}(t) with t​→𝑝​θ∗t\overset{p}{\to}\theta_{*}, and define

K^=(G^⊤​Wn​G^)−1​G^⊤​Wn,𝒱^=K^​S^​K^⊤.\widehat{K}=(\widehat{G}^{\top}W_{n}\widehat{G})^{-1}\widehat{G}^{\top}W_{n},\qquad\widehat{\mathcal{V}}=\widehat{K}\widehat{S}\widehat{K}^{\top}. (50)

Then 𝒱^​→𝑝​𝒱​(W)\widehat{\mathcal{V}}\overset{p}{\to}\mathcal{V}(W). The middle matrix is the consistent estimate of the actual joint moment covariance, rather than an arbitrary shrinkage target. For efficient family members, (G^⊤​S^−1​G^)−1(\widehat{G}^{\top}\widehat{S}^{-1}\widehat{G})^{-1} is also consistent for 𝒱∗\mathcal{V}_{*}. A Wald interval for a fixed nonzero contrast is

a⊤​θ^±z1−η/2​a⊤​𝒱^​a/M,η∈(0,1).a^{\top}\widehat{\theta}\ \pm\ z_{1-\eta/2}\sqrt{a^{\top}\widehat{\mathcal{V}}a/M},\qquad\eta\in(0,1). (51)

This interval has conditional asymptotic coverage 1−η1-\eta under the stated regular conditions.

The optional one-step approximation is first-order equivalent under the pilot conditions in Supplementary Section S1.2. The estimators in this paper are defined by the frozen-criterion minimization in Section 3.5.

Supplementary Section S1 gives detailed proofs of random-pilot covariance consistency, the influence expansion, all equality conditions, and the inference and one-step statements; further regular extremum-estimation background is provided by (Newey and McFadden, 1994).

5 Finite-Sample Calibration and the Half-Strength Default

Estimated covariance weights can give different finite-sample risks even when their limiting influence maps agree. For the CC-PPI estimator of Section 3.4, we examine the auxiliary penalty, the effect of covariance calibration on risk, and the choice of strength. Supplementary Sections S2–S4 contain the supporting results and proofs; numerical protocols are in Supplementary Section S5.

The exact parameter-risk analysis conditions on a fixed full-rank regression design and externally supplied predictions. Its structural calibration identities also apply to nonlinear moments. In correctly specified single-outcome regression with a covariate-measurable predictor, the population supervised–auxiliary cross covariance is zero, so calibration acts through the finite-sample criterion. The noisy-surrogate example in Section 6.3 illustrates the complementary regime with informative population cross covariance.

5.1 Auxiliary penalty in the GMM criterion

By Corollary 4.3, two regular family members with vanishing covariance perturbations satisfy M​(θ^(a)−θ^(b))=op​(1)\sqrt{M}(\widehat{\theta}^{(a)}-\widehat{\theta}^{(b)})=o_{p}(1). Comparing their finite-sample MSEs requires the higher-order contributions of covariance estimation, the sample auxiliary Jacobian and strength selection. Passing from distributional expansions to risk also requires moment control.

Higher-order GMM/GEL analyses retain contributions from moment/Jacobian dependence and estimated weights (Newey and Smith, 2004); variance estimation for linear two-step GMM may also need a finite-sample correction (Windmeijer, 2005). These results motivate retaining same-sample weight effects.

An exact decomposition explains one source of these differences. Partition any frozen positive definite weight as W=(Wj​k)j,k=12W=(W_{jk})_{j,k=1}^{2}, and put

ΛW=W11−1​W12,ΠW=W22−W21​W11−1​W12≻0.\Lambda_{W}=W_{11}^{-1}W_{12},\qquad\Pi_{W}=W_{22}-W_{21}W_{11}^{-1}W_{12}\succ 0. (52)

Completing the square yields

QW​(θ)=(m1+ΛW​m2)⊤​W11​(m1+ΛW​m2)+m2⊤​ΠW​m2.Q_{W}(\theta)=(m_{1}+\Lambda_{W}m_{2})^{\top}W_{11}(m_{1}+\Lambda_{W}m_{2})+m_{2}^{\top}\Pi_{W}m_{2}. (53)

For affine m2​(θ)=A5​θ−b2m_{2}(\theta)=A_{5}\theta-b_{2}, the second term has curvature A5⊤​ΠW​A5A_{5}^{\top}\Pi_{W}A_{5}. When A5A_{5} is invertible, it is a quadratic penalty around the root of m2=0m_{2}=0; otherwise it remains a penalty on the auxiliary moment, without requiring a unique anchor. Thus this penalty is a property of the full quadratic criterion. An equivalent estimating-equation representation can encode the same effect through its coefficients. Both ΛW\Lambda_{W} and ΠW\Pi_{W} change with the weight, so the penalty alone does not determine parameter risk. Under regular identical-covariate sampling, A5→p0A_{5}\to_{p}0; its finite-sample contribution is consequently not characterized by the limiting Jacobian G=(A⊤,0⊤)⊤G=(A^{\top},0^{\top})^{\top}.

For exact risk calculations, condition on full-column-rank X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, arbitrary U∈ℝN×dU\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}, and externally supplied finite predictions fL,fUf_{L},f_{U}. Let

Y\displaystyle Y =X​β+ϵ,C=(X⊤​X)−1​X⊤,t=C​Y,\displaystyle=X\beta+\epsilon,\quad C=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top},\quad t=CY, (54)
AL\displaystyle A_{L} =X⊤​X/n,AU=U⊤​U/N,H=(ALAU−AL),\displaystyle=X^{\top}X/n,\quad A_{U}=U^{\top}U/N,\quad H=\begin{pmatrix}A_{L}\\ A_{U}-A_{L}\end{pmatrix}, (55)
b\displaystyle b =(X⊤​Y/nU⊤​fU/N−X⊤​fL/n).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}X^{\top}Y/n\\ U^{\top}f_{U}/N-X^{\top}f_{L}/n\end{pmatrix}. (56)

Then g^​(θ)=H​θ−b\widehat{g}(\theta)=H\theta-b, and the complete frozen-weight solution is (30). The matrix HH has full column rank even if AU−ALA_{U}-A_{L} is singular. The predictor may be nonlinear in the covariates. Conditional parameter risk is R⁡(λ)=𝔼ϵ​‖β^λ−β‖2R(\lambda)=\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\|\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\beta\|^{2}. Random-design conclusions require averaging these conditional quantities with appropriate integrability; no dimension-growth claim is made here.

5.2 Covariance calibration and finite-sample risk

Write ρ=n/N\rho=n/N and use the nn-scaled covariance 𝖲=S^/c1,n\mathsf{S}=\widehat{S}/c_{1,n}. Its scores are those in (9). With CL=Cov^ℒ​(h,h)C_{L}=\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{L}}(h,h), CU=Cov^𝒰​(hU,hU)C_{U}=\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{U}}(h^{U},h^{U}), and η=εM/c1,n>0\eta=\varepsilon_{M}/c_{1,n}>0,

𝖲=Cov^ℒ​(s−h)+diag⁡(0,ρ​CU)+η​I2​d.\mathsf{S}=\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathcal{L}}\begin{pmatrix}s\\ -h\end{pmatrix}+\operatorname{diag}(0,\rho C_{U})+\eta I_{2d}. (57)

Multiplication of the full covariance by a positive scalar leaves its GMM minimizer unchanged. In this section, QQ denotes the nn-scaled criterion, namely c1,nc_{1,n} times the criterion in Section 3. In the experiments below, N≥nN\geq n, c1,n=1c_{1,n}=1, and η=n−2\eta=n^{-2}.

Let c=m1+m2c=m_{1}+m_{2} denote the prediction-corrected moment, and introduce

Bc=(II0I),T=(I−I),Bc​𝖲​Bc⊤=(VcRcRc⊤Dc),Ω=Dc−Rc⊤​Vc−1​Rc.B_{c}=\begin{pmatrix}I&I\\ 0&I\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}I\\ -I\end{pmatrix},\quad B_{c}\mathsf{S}B_{c}^{\top}=\begin{pmatrix}V_{c}&R_{c}\\ R_{c}^{\top}&D_{c}\end{pmatrix},\quad\Omega=D_{c}-R_{c}^{\top}V_{c}^{-1}R_{c}. (58)

Both VcV_{c} and Ω\Omega are positive definite: the calibration principle is to retain the corrected channel (Vc,Rc)(V_{c},R_{c}) while changing the auxiliary residual metric.

5.2.1 Unlabeled prediction-score covariance

The unlabeled sample supplies information for calibrating the prediction-score covariance within the auxiliary block. Under the regular pilot laws, CU−CL→p0C_{U}-C_{L}\to_{p}0, preserving the efficient limit. At finite samples, its joint dependence with the pilot and estimated weight is retained in the signed transfer analysis of Section 5.2.3. Centered divisors also enter that analysis: at an external deterministic pilot, 𝔼​CL=(1−1/n)​Σh​h\mathbb{E}C_{L}=(1-1/n)\Sigma_{hh} and 𝔼​CU=(1−1/N)​Σh​h\mathbb{E}C_{U}=(1-1/N)\Sigma_{hh}. The target preserves the common population limit while changing the estimated auxiliary covariance at finite sample sizes.

5.2.2 Channel-preserving targets

We first characterize targets that preserve the corrected channel.

Proposition 5.1 (Channel-preserving calibration).

A symmetric positive definite target 𝖲∗\mathsf{S}_{*} preserves the first block row (Vc,Rc)(V_{c},R_{c}) in (58) if and only if

𝖲∗=𝖲+T​K​T⊤,K=K⊤,Ω+K≻0.\mathsf{S}_{*}=\mathsf{S}+TKT^{\top},\qquad K=K^{\top},\qquad\Omega+K\succ 0. (59)

For every such target, including nonlinear moments, its criterion is exactly

QK​(θ)=c​(θ)⊤​Vc−1​c​(θ)+rc​(θ)⊤​(Ω+K)−1​rc​(θ),rc=m2−Rc⊤​Vc−1​c.Q_{K}(\theta)=c(\theta)^{\top}V_{c}^{-1}c(\theta)+r_{c}(\theta)^{\top}(\Omega+K)^{-1}r_{c}(\theta),\quad r_{c}=m_{2}-R_{c}^{\top}V_{c}^{-1}c. (60)
Proof.

The transformed covariance difference must be diag⁡(0,K)\operatorname{diag}(0,K). Since Bc​T=(0,−I)⊤B_{c}T=(0,-I)^{\top}, transforming back gives (59), with unique KK. Positive definiteness is equivalent to Ω+K≻0\Omega+K\succ 0 by the Schur complement. The block inverse gives (60). ∎

We choose within this class using two requirements on the covariance information. Together they identify a unique raw target once the pool is fixed. They specify the construction rather than a risk-optimality criterion or a data-budget allocation.

P1 (preserve the corrected channel).

The target keeps the first block row (Vc,Rc)(V_{c},R_{c}) of the corrected criterion; only the metric attached to the auxiliary residual may change.

P2 (calibrate that metric with the unlabeled prediction covariance).

In the auxiliary block, the labeled prediction covariance CLC_{L} is replaced by a pool F⁡(CL,CU)F(C_{L},C_{U}) built from the unlabeled sample, while the sample-size term ρ​CU\rho C_{U} and the ridge η​I\eta I are left unchanged.

Proposition 5.2 (The principles force the target).

Fix 𝖲\mathsf{S} with blocks as in (58), and let F⁡(CL,CU)F(C_{L},C_{U}) be any symmetric prediction-covariance pool. Let 𝖲∗\mathsf{S}_{*} satisfy P1 together with

P2′: the auxiliary block of Bc𝖲∗Bc⊤ equals F(CL,CU)+ρCU+ηI.\text{P2${}^{\prime}$: the auxiliary block of }B_{c}\mathsf{S}_{*}B_{c}^{\top}\text{ equals }F(C_{L},C_{U})+\rho C_{U}+\eta I.

Then the unique symmetric candidate is

𝖲∗=𝖲+T​KF​T⊤,KF=F⁡(CL,CU)−CL;\mathsf{S}_{*}=\mathsf{S}+TK_{F}T^{\top},\qquad K_{F}=F(C_{L},C_{U})-C_{L}; (61)

it is a positive definite target if and only if Ω+KF≻0\Omega+K_{F}\succ 0, and its criterion is (60) with K=KFK=K_{F}. For the pool F=CUF=C_{U} the auxiliary block becomes (1+ρ)​CU+η​I(1+\rho)C_{U}+\eta I, its population shape, and KF=CU−CLK_{F}=C_{U}-C_{L}.

Proof.

By Proposition 5.1, P1 holds if and only if 𝖲∗=𝖲+T​K​T⊤\mathsf{S}_{*}=\mathsf{S}+TKT^{\top} for a unique symmetric KK with Ω+K≻0\Omega+K\succ 0. Since Bc​T=(0,−I)⊤B_{c}T=(0,-I)^{\top}, the corrected blocks of 𝖲+T​K​T⊤\mathsf{S}+TKT^{\top} are (Vc,Rc,Dc+K)(V_{c},R_{c},D_{c}+K), so P2′ is equivalent to Dc+K=F⁡(CL,CU)+ρ​CU+η​ID_{c}+K=F(C_{L},C_{U})+\rho C_{U}+\eta I. With Dc=CL+ρ​CU+η​ID_{c}=C_{L}+\rho C_{U}+\eta I this gives (61), and positive definiteness is the Schur condition Ω+KF≻0\Omega+K_{F}\succ 0. ∎

Once the pool is fixed, P1 and P2 determine the target. We take F=CUF=C_{U}. Replacing the labeled prediction-covariance contribution CLC_{L} by CUC_{U}, while preserving the corrected channel, gives the raw correction

K=CU−CL,Δ=T⁡(CU−CL)​T⊤,K=C_{U}-C_{L},\qquad\Delta=T(C_{U}-C_{L})T^{\top}, (62)

and the target (27) is (62) after the spectral protection that follows.

Apply the spectral protection of (22) to the raw correction. Here h=1/2h=1/2 denotes the default strength and κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 the spectral cap. Protection retains the form Δp=T​Kp​T⊤\Delta_{p}=TK_{p}T^{\top}, so the frozen criterion along the implemented path is

Qλ=c⊤​Vc−1​c+rc⊤​(Ω+λ​Kp)−1​rc.Q_{\lambda}=c^{\top}V_{c}^{-1}c+r_{c}^{\top}(\Omega+\lambda K_{p})^{-1}r_{c}. (63)

The low-rank protection formula and its admissibility properties are given in Supplementary Section S2.4. Under the covariance consistency conditions of Section 4.1, the calibrated path satisfies

sup0≤λ≤1∥S^λ−S^∥→p0.\sup_{0\leq\lambda\leq 1}\|\widehat{S}_{\lambda}-\widehat{S}\|\to_{p}0. (64)

Corollary 4.3 therefore gives the common efficient limit for the half-strength estimator.

Theorem 5.3 (Signed finite-sample transfer).

In every parameter dimension dd, for the actual same-data pipeline,

R⁡(h)−R⁡(0)\displaystyle R(h)-R(0) =𝒟+2​𝔼​⟨g⟂,u⟂⟩+Qu,\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}+2\mathbb{E}\langle g_{\perp},u_{\perp}\rangle+Q_{u}, (68)

Proof.

𝔼​z=0\mathbb{E}z=0 and 𝔼​z​z⊤=I\mathbb{E}zz^{\top}=I. The projection residuals have zero means and are orthogonal to zz. Substitute β^0−β=ag+(J+Ag)​z+g⟂\widehat{\beta}_{0}-\beta=a_{g}+(J+A_{g})z+g_{\perp} into 2​𝔼​⟨β^0−β,u⟩+𝔼​‖u‖22\mathbb{E}\langle\widehat{\beta}_{0}-\beta,u\rangle+\mathbb{E}\|u\|^{2}. Orthogonality gives (68); Cauchy–Schwarz gives (69). ∎

The first two terms of 𝒟\mathcal{D} measure the change in squared mean bias; the others measure the change in linear noise response and its correlation with the original fit. The bound controls only the residual nonlinear interaction by magnitude. A reduction in linear noise response can therefore lower MSE even without reducing bias. The sufficient condition concerns expected loss and involves population quantities that require separate estimation.

The calibration and pilot use the same response throughout this identity. Supplementary Sections S2.6 and S3.1 derive the quadratic score-covariance representation and Gaussian conditional-projection refinements. We next give design conditions under which the implemented calibration improves risk, allowing prediction error.

5.2.4 A design-based improvement result

The following result establishes a favorable calibration direction under explicit design conditions, including the same-response pilot and active spectral protection. Throughout this finite-sample analysis the regression fit is unconstrained, with parameter space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Theorem 5.4 (Design-dependent improvement and prediction-error tolerance).

Consider scalar regression without an intercept, with fixed labeled and unlabeled covariates in {0,−a,a}\{0,-a,a\}, a>0a>0. Let m≥2m\geq 2 and MUM_{U} be their numbers of nonzero rows, and put p=m/np=m/n, u=MU/Nu=M_{U}/N, with 0<u<p<10<u<p<1. Let Yi=β​xi+ϵiY_{i}=\beta x_{i}+\epsilon_{i}, where the errors are independent N⁡(0,σ2)N(0,\sigma^{2}), σ>0\sigma>0, and let f⁡(x)=α​xf(x)=\alpha x. Use the centered divisors n,Nn,N, the OLS pilot, any fixed η>0\eta>0, cap κ=1/2\kappa=1/2, and the complete fit along (S2.5). Write μ=β−α\mu=\beta-\alpha and Rμ​(λ)=𝔼μ​(β^λ−β)2R_{\mu}(\lambda)=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}(\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\beta)^{2}.

At μ=0\mu=0, the risk is strictly decreasing in λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] if p+u<1p+u<1, strictly increasing if p+u>1p+u>1, and constant if p+u=1p+u=1. In particular, the first case gives 𝒢ref=R0​(0)−R0​(h)>0\mathcal{G}_{\rm ref}=R_{0}(0)-R_{0}(h)>0 for h=1/2h=1/2.

For this favorable case, set s2=σ2/(m​a2)s^{2}=\sigma^{2}/(ma^{2}) and define, under μ=0\mu=0,

Hh2=𝔼0​{[(β^h−α)2−(β^0−α)2]2},Jh2=𝔼0​(β^h−β^0)2.H_{h}^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{0}\{[(\widehat{\beta}_{h}-\alpha)^{2}-(\widehat{\beta}_{0}-\alpha)^{2}]^{2}\},\qquad J_{h}^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{0}(\widehat{\beta}_{h}-\widehat{\beta}_{0})^{2}. (70)

These constants are finite and have explicit Gaussian/chi-square integral expressions in Supplementary Section S3.5. With q=μ2/s2q=\mu^{2}/s^{2}, put

εh​(μ)=Hh​cosh⁡(q)−1+2​|μ|​Jh​sinh⁡(q).\varepsilon_{h}(\mu)=H_{h}\sqrt{\cosh(q)-1}+2|\mu|J_{h}\sqrt{\sinh(q)}. (71)

Then

Rμ​(0)−Rμ​(h)≥𝒢ref−εh​(μ).R_{\mu}(0)-R_{\mu}(h)\geq\mathcal{G}_{\rm ref}-\varepsilon_{h}(\mu). (72)

Consequently εh​(μ)<𝒢ref\varepsilon_{h}(\mu)<\mathcal{G}_{\rm ref} is a quantitative sufficient condition for strict improvement. It holds on a nonempty neighborhood of μ=0\mu=0.

Proof.

The three-point design makes the supervised/auxiliary sample cross covariance vanish exactly at the actual OLS pilot. The resulting scalar rational fit has a pointwise loss derivative whose sign is that of (u−p)​(1−u−p)(u-p)(1-u-p). Supplementary Section S3.5 derives this formula and the Gaussian/chi-square laws. Joint reflection of the pilot error and OLS residual leaves the covariance unchanged and reverses the centered fit. The even and odd parts of the Gaussian likelihood ratio then give (71)–(72); Supplementary Section S3.6 proves the corresponding result in every fixed parameter dimension. ∎

Theorem 5.4 supplies improvement from explicit design and predictor conditions with noisy responses. At the favorable reference model the risk decreases along the path, so half strength captures part of its available gain; Supplementary Section S3.5 derives the path optimum. The Gaussian-shift argument extends improvement to a neighborhood measured in pilot-standard-error units, and Supplementary Section S3.7 gives stability under small design and prediction perturbations. Positive ridge supports this fixed-design analysis even when the limiting auxiliary covariance is singular.

5.3 The half-strength default

For the strength decision below, R∗path=infλ∈[0,1]R⁡(λ)R_{*}^{\rm path}=\inf_{\lambda\in[0,1]}R(\lambda) denotes the smallest risk over deterministic strengths on the prescribed path.

Half strength combines a stable covariance blend with a simple strength rule. With κ=1/2\kappa=1/2, relative covariance eigenvalues lie in [3/4,5/4][3/4,5/4]. Proposition S4.5 gives the scalar population balance for half strength, and the following quadratic decision model provides its midpoint minimax-regret rationale.

Proposition 5.5 (Midpoint as a minimax-regret strength).

Fix the design and the predictor. Consider a quadratic decision model with excess-risk curves ℰζ​(λ)=B​(λ−ζ)2\mathcal{E}_{\zeta}(\lambda)=B(\lambda-\zeta)^{2}, where B>0B>0 is known and the unknown optimal strength ζ\zeta lies in [l,u]⊆[0,1][l,u]\subseteq[0,1]. Then for every deterministic λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] the worst-case excess risk over that interval is

W⁡(λ)=supζ∈[l,u]ℰζ​(λ)=B​max⁡{(λ−l)2,(λ−u)2},W(\lambda)=\sup_{\zeta\in[l,u]}\mathcal{E}_{\zeta}(\lambda)=B\max\{(\lambda-l)^{2},(\lambda-u)^{2}\}, (73)

which is uniquely minimized at λ=(l+u)/2\lambda=(l+u)/2 with value B​(u−l)2/4B(u-l)^{2}/4. In particular, if the uncertainty interval is symmetric about 1/21/2 then the minimax-regret strength is exactly 1/21/2 and its worst-case excess risk is B​(u−l)2/4B(u-l)^{2}/4. If instead ζ\zeta has a prior with mean mm and variance AπA_{\pi} on [l,u][l,u], then 𝔼π​{ℰζ​(λ)}=B⁡{(λ−m)2+Aπ}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\{\mathcal{E}_{\zeta}(\lambda)\}=B\{(\lambda-m)^{2}+A_{\pi}\}, minimized at λ=m\lambda=m; a uniform prior gives the midpoint again, with average excess B​(u−l)2/12B(u-l)^{2}/12.

The proposition gives the deterministic-strength decision under quadratic excess risk. The quadratic form is exact for affine-in-strength paths, including zero scalar feedback; the complete CC-PPI path is analyzed below through its rational representation. Selecting strength from the response requires a risk estimate whose behavior after selection must also be accounted for (Tibshirani and Rosset, 2019; Cauchois et al., 2021).

Half strength avoids response-based tuning. For comparison, Supplementary Section S3.3 analyzes a paired parameter-SURE selector and bounds its selection error. We now compare the default with the best fixed strength on the same path.

Let

R∗path=inf0≤λ≤1R⁡(λ),Gh=R⁡(h)−R∗path,G0=R⁡(0)−R∗path.R_{*}^{\rm path}=\inf_{0\leq\lambda\leq 1}R(\lambda),\qquad G_{h}=R(h)-R_{*}^{\rm path},\qquad G_{0}=R(0)-R_{*}^{\rm path}. (74)

Here GhG_{h} is the risk forfeited by the default relative to the best deterministic strength on the prescribed path. R⁡(h)−R⁡(0)=Gh−G0,Gh≥0,G0≥0.R(h)-R(0)=G_{h}-G_{0},\qquad G_{h}\geq 0,\quad G_{0}\geq 0. (75)

The recovered-gain fraction 1−Gh/G01-G_{h}/G_{0} is interpretable only when G0>0G_{0}>0, and lies in [0,1][0,1] only if the default improves on the original fit.

An exact representation makes continuum comparisons possible. For each observed response set

The moment assumptions hold at fixed full-rank design, positive ridge and Gaussian errors for the actual estimator.

The truncation order controls the risk-approximation error without treating the estimated weight as independent of the response. The numerical comparison below estimates risk by Monte Carlo evaluation of the exact strength path. Supplementary Section S4.6 records the remainder analysis, and Proposition S4.4 shows that the rational realized-loss path can be nonconvex.

We evaluated the specified path under correlated Gaussian covariates, Σi​j=0.6|i−j|\Sigma_{ij}=0.6^{|i-j|}, unit Gaussian response noise, and an external linear predictor with normalized slope discrepancy rr. The eight laws combine d∈{2,5}d\in\{2,5\}, n∈{40,160}n\in\{40,160\}, r∈{0.2,0.5}r\in\{0.2,0.5\} and N=5​nN=5n. Each law uses 16 designs; paired discrepancies share covariates. Two independent streams of 4,000 responses fit fixed-strength diagnostic references on a 101-point grid; a third stream of 8,000 responses evaluates risk. The references use simulation truth and are not feasible selectors. Table 1 reports averages of designwise OLS-normalized risks, using the exact conditional OLS risk tr⁡[(X⊤​X)−1]\operatorname{tr}[(X^{\top}X)^{-1}].

Half improves on original GMM-PPI in all eight law averages in Table 1. Independent fixed-strength references improve further by only 1.30–2.57% of half-strength risk. Approximate simultaneous Monte Carlo bands with the curvature correction give upper endpoints at most 3.03% for the sampled-design average gap. Grid and reference-fitting diagnostics are much smaller than the measured gaps. Thus the independently selected reference leaves little further risk reduction on these paths; Supplementary Section S5.4 records the uncertainty and reference protocol.

6 Simulation Studies

We compare parameter MSE in linear and logistic regression, separating the gain from the full GMM fit from the additional gain due to covariance calibration. A multi-outcome noisy-surrogate example compares the population efficiencies of unrestricted, diagonal and scalar corrections.

6.1 Setup and methods

In the regression simulations, X∼N⁡(0,Σ)X\sim N(0,\Sigma) with Σi​j=0.6|i−j|\Sigma_{ij}=0.6^{|i-j|} and d∈{2,5,10,20}d\in\{2,5,10,20\}. We draw one labeled and one unlabeled design per cell and seed, with N=5​nN=5n, then repeat responses on those fixed designs. There are two design seeds. Linear regression uses Y=X​β+ϵY=X\beta+\epsilon, ϵ∼N⁡(0,1)\epsilon\sim N(0,1), ‖β‖=1\|\beta\|=1, and f⁡(x)=x⊤​αf(x)=x^{\top}\alpha with α=β+r​𝟏d/𝟏d⊤​Σ​𝟏d\alpha=\beta+r\mathbf{1}_{d}/\sqrt{\mathbf{1}_{d}^{\top}\Sigma\mathbf{1}_{d}}. The grid is n∈{50,100,500,1000,2000,10000}n\in\{50,100,500,1000,2000,10000\} and r∈{.2,.5,1}r\in\{.2,.5,1\}, with 1,000 responses per design. Logistic regression uses Pr⁡(Y=1∣X)=expit⁡(X⊤​θ)\Pr(Y=1\mid X)=\operatorname{expit}(X^{\top}\theta), where θ=0.6​b/‖b‖\theta=0.6b/\|b\|, b1=1b_{1}=1, b2=0.5b_{2}=0.5 and bj=0.4​(−0.6)j−1b_{j}=0.4(-0.6)^{j-1} for j≥3j\geq 3. Its predictor is f⁡(x)=expit⁡(x⊤​α)f(x)=\operatorname{expit}(x^{\top}\alpha) with α=θ+r​𝟏d/𝟏d⊤​Σ​𝟏d\alpha=\theta+r\mathbf{1}_{d}/\sqrt{\mathbf{1}_{d}^{\top}\Sigma\mathbf{1}_{d}}. It uses n∈{100,500,2000}n\in\{100,500,2000\}, r∈{.2,.5}r\in\{.2,.5\} and 200 responses per design.

Comparators are supervised estimation, original PPI, PPI++, PSPA, PDC and original GMM-PPI. PSPA uses the full-Jacobian one-step update, with a lower-capped version retained as a sensitivity check. The PPI++ covariance plug-in is evaluated at the supervised pilot. Linear moments have closed-form solutions, and logistic fits use damped score solving and trust-region GMM least squares. Strength grids contain 101 linear points and 11 logistic points. Full numerical protocols, additional configurations and convergence diagnostics are in Supplementary Section S5.4.

6.2 Single-outcome linear regression

Table 2 reports the small-sample comparison at r=.2r=.2, including n=50n=50 and n/dn/d as low as 2.52.5. At d=20,n=50d=20,n=50, CC-PPI has 53.3% of supervised MSE, compared with 55.3% for original GMM-PPI; at d=10,n=50d=10,n=50, the corresponding ratios are 57.2% and 58.5%. GMM-PPI and CC-PPI produce substantial reductions, particularly at smaller labeled sizes. At d=20,n=100d=20,n=100, CC-PPI has 52.8% of supervised MSE, compared with 54.3% for original GMM-PPI. At d=10,n=500d=10,n=500, calibration lowers the ratio from 76.4% to 74.7%. The reductions become smaller as the labeled sample grows, consistent with the common first-order limit. The correctly specified conditional mean gives zero population supervised–auxiliary cross covariance here, so the observed gains arise from the finite-sample criterion.

The bias–variance decomposition shows a modest squared bias alongside a substantial variance reduction. At n=50n=50, GMM-PPI variance is 57.1% of supervised MSE, rising to 95.7% at n=10000n=10000. This bias–variance tradeoff is consistent with finite-sample shrinkage.

6.3 Multi-outcome surrogate model

We now extend the predictor-of-XX setting to an observed surrogate available in both inference samples. Let pp be the covariate dimension and qq the number of outcomes, so the parameter dimension is d=p​qd=pq. Take Y=X​Θ+ϵY=X\Theta+\epsilon and the supplied surrogate Y^=X​Θ+η\widehat{Y}=X\Theta+\eta, where η=Γ​ϵ+ξ/2\eta=\Gamma\epsilon+\xi/2, Γ=Iq+.8​(𝟏q​𝟏q⊤−Iq)\Gamma=I_{q}+.8(\mathbf{1}_{q}\mathbf{1}_{q}^{\top}-I_{q}), and independent ϵ,ξ\epsilon,\xi have covariance Σϵ=(1−ρe)​Iq+ρe​𝟏q​𝟏q⊤\Sigma_{\epsilon}=(1-\rho_{e})I_{q}+\rho_{e}\mathbf{1}_{q}\mathbf{1}_{q}^{\top}. The joint law of the covariates and surrogate is common to the two inference samples. The surrogate contains information beyond the displayed regression covariates and is not a deterministic function of them.

Using feature-major score vectorization and rs=n/N=1/5r_{s}=n/N=1/5, the population score blocks and Jacobian inverse are

V=ΣX⊗Σϵ,C=ΣX⊗(Σϵ​Γ⊤),D=(1+rs)​ΣX⊗(Γ​Σϵ​Γ⊤+Σϵ/4),J−1=ΣX−1⊗Iq.V=\Sigma_{X}\otimes\Sigma_{\epsilon},\quad C=\Sigma_{X}\otimes(\Sigma_{\epsilon}\Gamma^{\top}),\quad D=(1+r_{s})\Sigma_{X}\otimes(\Gamma\Sigma_{\epsilon}\Gamma^{\top}+\Sigma_{\epsilon}/4),\quad J^{-1}=\Sigma_{X}^{-1}\otimes I_{q}. (84)

For W=J−⁣⊤​J−1W=J^{-\top}J^{-1}, all three classes minimize the same parameter trace risk. Their coefficients are

L∗=C​D−1,ω∗=(W∘D)−1​diag⁡(C⊤​W),ℓ∗=tr⁡(W​C)/tr⁡(W​D),L_{*}=CD^{-1},\qquad\omega_{*}=(W\circ D)^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(C^{\top}W),\qquad\ell_{*}={\operatorname{tr}(WC)}/{\operatorname{tr}(WD)}, (85)

where ∘\circ is the entrywise product, the diagonal class uses Diag⁡(ω∗)\operatorname{Diag}(\omega_{*}), and diag\operatorname{diag} here extracts a vector. The expressions follow by differentiating the quadratic trace risk. Covariances are computed analytically; no Monte Carlo approximation or truncation of L∗L_{*} is used. The nested-class ordering is full ≤\leq diagonal ≤\leq scalar.

The full correction gains efficiency by using cross-outcome information. In this symmetric surrogate model, the diagonal and scalar optima coincide; the full matrix improves on both. At ρe=.7\rho_{e}=.7, their relative excess risk rises to approximately .332, 1.455 and 3.432 percent for q=2,3,5q=2,3,5. The unrestricted optimum in Section 4 uses this cross-outcome information.

6.4 Logistic regression

Table 5 shows that the finite-sample accuracy gains extend to nonlinear logistic moments. As in linear regression, most of the MSE reduction comes from the full GMM fit, with calibration making a smaller additional change. The reported sizes use the convergence-checked fits and all 200 paired responses in each supervised denominator. Supplementary Section S5.4 records the smaller-size solver diagnostics.

7 Real-Data Studies

7.1 Setup and methods

We study four datasets with externally trained XGBoost predictors (Chen and Guestrin, 2016). California Housing uses a northern training region and a southern evaluation region; Bike Sharing uses an earlier training period and a later evaluation period; ACS Income trains on 2018 and evaluates on 2019; Wine Quality trains on red wine and evaluates on white wine. The shift is between predictor training and inference, whereas labeled and unlabeled inference points are random disjoint subsets of the same evaluation region. The target uses a specified low-dimensional covariate subset, and the predictor may use additional observed features.

For each labeled size, we evaluate 50 random subsets per seed, with two seeds (100 evaluation subsamples total). The target is the supervised parameter on the complete evaluation region, using the empirical-target convention of (Ji et al., 2026). All estimators use the same labeled subset and unlabeled complement. The externally fitted prediction rules are held fixed across inference subsets. Outcomes, feature selection, preprocessing and predictor settings are given in Supplementary Section S5.3.

The main tables report sizes for which the supervised pilot and solver checks support an accuracy comparison. The extended sample-size grid, method-specific failure counts and stability profiles are reported in Supplementary Section S5.4; a dagger in a main table denotes a failed fit or an unavailable ratio.

The fixed-strength reference CC-PPIref selects a strength on 50 separate training subsamples using the full-region target, then evaluates it on the common 100 fresh subsamples. It uses 101 linear grid points and 11 logistic points. This independent reference measures the remaining accuracy available along the calibration path.

7.2 Estimation accuracy

Figure 1 compares the methods across labeled sample sizes. Tables 7–10 report selected sizes, starting at n=25n=25 for California Housing and Wine Quality and n=75n=75 for ACS Income. Supplementary Section S5.4 retains the complete grid and convergence diagnostics.

CC-PPI produces substantial gains over supervised estimation in all four tasks at the reported sizes. At n=500n=500, its MSE ratios are 68.9% on California Housing, 17.4% on Bike Sharing, 86.0% on ACS Income and 67.9% on Wine Quality. Calibration lowers the MSE of the corresponding original GMM fits. On Wine Quality, CC-PPI outperforms PDC at n=50n=50 (45.1% versus 286.4%), whereas PDC is better at n=2000n=2000 (53.8% versus 65.8%). The crossover shows that the small-sample advantage need not persist as the labeled sample grows. Original PPI is especially effective on California Housing, so the relative performance also depends on how the predictor information enters the estimator.

The independent reference gives a measure of the accuracy left beyond half strength. At n=2000n=2000, the default/reference ratios are 69.4/65.3 on California Housing, 14.7/14.7 on Bike Sharing and 65.8/62.8 on Wine Quality. The default is close to the independently selected strength in these comparisons.

8 Conclusion

CC-PPI calibrates the GMM covariance weight using unlabeled prediction scores. The raw target preserves the corrected channel and replaces the labeled prediction-covariance contribution in the auxiliary residual metric with its unlabeled counterpart. Spectral protection makes the covariance positive definite, and half strength fixes the blend without response-based tuning. Under the regular fixed-moment conditions, the calibration preserves first-order efficiency.

For linear regression, the finite-sample risk identities retain the dependence among the pilot, empirical covariance and final estimate. The primitive design theorem proves improvement with a quantified tolerance to prediction error. The quadratic midpoint decision model motivates half strength, while the exact path and convergent risk approximation quantify its distance from the best fixed strength.

The regression simulations show substantial MSE reductions from the full GMM criterion, with calibration often improving the fit further. Four real-data studies extend the comparison to externally trained predictors under spatial, temporal and wine-type shifts. In the dedicated path experiments, independent fixed-strength references leave only a few percent of further risk reduction; the linear real-data comparisons also put the default close to the reference.

Further work could establish broader design conditions for improvement, compare other auxiliary residual metrics, and develop finite-sample interval calibration.

Appendix S1 Regular GMM Limits and Efficiency

S1.1 Additional covariance targets and a benchmark strength

We give three alternative covariance targets. The cross-block target is

S0,ncross=diag⁡(V^,D^).S_{0,n}^{\mathrm{cross}}=\operatorname{diag}(\widehat{V},\widehat{D}). (S1.1)

It retains within-block covariances and yields

S^λcross=(V^−(1−λ)​R^−(1−λ)​R^⊤D^).\widehat{S}_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{cross}}=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat{V}&-(1-\lambda)\widehat{R}\\ -(1-\lambda)\widehat{R}^{\top}&\widehat{D}\end{pmatrix}. (S1.2)

Thus estimated cross covariance is discounted while the two diagonal blocks remain unchanged.

The spherical target is

S0,nsph=diag⁡{tr⁡(V^)d​Id,tr⁡(D^)d​Id}.S_{0,n}^{\mathrm{sph}}=\operatorname{diag}\left\{\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\widehat{V})}{d}I_{d},\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\widehat{D})}{d}I_{d}\right\}. (S1.3)

It changes both the cross block and within-block eigenvalue dispersion. This target depends on the units of moment coordinates; rescaling those coordinates can change the estimator.

The diagonal target is

S0,ndiag=diag⁡{Diag⁡(V^),Diag⁡(D^)},S_{0,n}^{\mathrm{diag}}=\operatorname{diag}\{\operatorname{Diag}(\widehat{V}),\operatorname{Diag}(\widehat{D})\}, (S1.4)

where Diag⁡(K)\operatorname{Diag}(K) extracts the diagonal into a diagonal matrix, and diag⁡(K1,K2)\operatorname{diag}(K_{1},K_{2}) denotes block concatenation. This target preserves marginal variances but depends on the coordinate axes.

Other choices include metric-based targets and their combinations. For the targets above, a sample-size benchmark strength is

λn=min⁡{λmax,c​d/n},0<λmax<1,c>0,\lambda_{n}=\min\{\lambda_{\max},c\,d/n\},\qquad 0<\lambda_{\max}<1,\quad c>0, (S1.5)

with c=1c=1 and λmax=0.8\lambda_{\max}=0.8 as a concrete choice. This benchmark depends on dimension and labeled sample size. It does not estimate prediction quality or parameter risk; its first-order limit and finite-sample performance require separate analyses.

S1.2 Optional one-step computation

As an optional computational approximation to the estimator defined in (18), a single Gauss–Newton update from tt is

θ^λ,αone=t−{J^​(t)⊤​Wλ,α​J^​(t)}−1​J^​(t)⊤​Wλ,α​g^​(t).\widehat{\theta}_{\lambda,\alpha}^{\mathrm{one}}=t-\{\widehat{J}(t)^{\top}W_{\lambda,\alpha}\widehat{J}(t)\}^{-1}\widehat{J}(t)^{\top}W_{\lambda,\alpha}\widehat{g}(t). (S1.6)

It equals the unconstrained solution for affine moments of full column rank. For nonlinear moments it is a separate finite-sample implementation; first-order equivalence requires the regularity and initialization conditions of the asymptotic analysis. Unless stated otherwise, the family denotes minimization of the frozen criterion, rather than this single update.

Proposition S1.1 (One-step first-order equivalence).

Suppose (R2)–(R4), the joint moment limit, and M​(t−θ∗)=Op​(1)\sqrt{M}(t-\theta_{*})=O_{p}(1) hold. The one-step update in (S1.6) has the expansion (34). If a full minimizer also satisfies Theorem 4.1, the update and that minimizer differ by op(M−1/2)o_{p}(M^{-1/2}).

Proof.

Uniform Jacobian convergence and the pilot rate imply g^(t)=g^(θ∗)+G(t−θ∗)+op(M−1/2)\widehat{g}(t)=\widehat{g}(\theta_{*})+G(t-\theta_{*})+o_{p}(M^{-1/2}). The update coefficient converges to K⁡(W)K(W), and K⁡(W)​G=IdK(W)G=I_{d}. Substitution cancels the pilot error to first order and gives the claimed expansion. ∎

For nonlinear moments, first-order equivalence allows finite-sample differences between the two procedures. Risk comparisons also require moment bounds beyond the distributional expansion. The finite-sample analysis therefore uses the specified estimator and solver throughout.

This supplement gives the details underlying Sections 3–5. Expectations in the asymptotic analysis are conditional on the external predictor. Finite-sample regression expectations additionally condition on X,U,fL,fUX,U,f_{L},f_{U}. Vector norms are Euclidean and matrix norms without a subscript are operator norms. A covariance consistency assertion is distinct from a risk assertion. Classical GMM and extremum-estimation foundations are provided by (Hansen, 1982; Newey and McFadden, 1994); the derivations below specialize them to the stated moment structure and frozen, possibly same-data weights.

S1.3 Identification, covariance, and the joint central limit theorem

Identical covariate marginals imply 𝔼​m2​(θ)=0\mathbb{E}m_{2}(\theta)=0 for each fixed θ\theta. Under valid differentiation under the expectation, its population derivative is zero. This does not set its observed sample derivative to zero. At θ∗\theta_{*}, let

ai=(ψi−(hi−𝔼​h)),bj=(0hjU−𝔼​h).a_{i}=\begin{pmatrix}\psi_{i}\\ -(h_{i}-\mathbb{E}h)\end{pmatrix},\qquad b_{j}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ h_{j}^{U}-\mathbb{E}h\end{pmatrix}. (S1.7)

All means and cross-block signs in this calculation use the sign convention of (4).

At a random consistent pilot tt, let F^n​(θ)\widehat{F}_{n}(\theta) be any empirical score mean or score second-product matrix used in the covariance. The imposed uniform laws imply

‖F^n​(t)−F⁡(θ∗)‖≤supθ∈𝒩‖F^n​(θ)−F⁡(θ)‖+|F⁡(t)−F⁡(θ∗)|=op​(1),\|\widehat{F}_{n}(t)-F(\theta_{*})\|\leq\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal{N}}\|\widehat{F}_{n}(\theta)-F(\theta)\|+\|F(t)-F(\theta_{*})\|=o_{p}(1), (S1.8)
