Appendix S2 Calibration and Regularity

S2.1 Finite-sample rates

The following rate statement concerns random designs; subsequent exact risk calculations condition on a realized full-rank design. Assume fixed dimension, independent identically distributed covariate samples with N/nN/n bounded below, and finite second moments of X​X⊤XX^{\top} and X​f​(X)Xf(X). These are fourth-moment requirements on the relevant quadratic design scores. For the affine regression moments, empirical coefficient bounds then hold uniformly on compact parameter sets. Assume also a regular positive definite covariance limit and a consistent root-nn baseline fit. For the risk expansion below, impose the stated L2L^{2} remainder bounds; distributional orders alone do not imply risk orders.

Proposition S2.1 (Scales of the finite-sample choice).

Under these conditions:

  1. (a)

    A5=Op(n−1/2)A_{5}=O_{p}(n^{-1/2}) and m2(θ)=Op(n−1/2)m_{2}(\theta)=O_{p}(n^{-1/2}) uniformly on compact sets. For weights with bounded Schur complements, m2⊤​ΠW​m2=Op​(n−1)m_{2}^{\top}\Pi_{W}m_{2}=O_{p}(n^{-1}).

  2. (b)

    Let the whitened update have amplitude at most a deterministic γn<1\gamma_{n}<1, bounded away from one. On a uniformly well-conditioned affine fit path, β^λ−β^0=Op(γnn−1/2)\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\widehat{\beta}_{0}=O_{p}(\gamma_{n}n^{-1/2}) uniformly for 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq 1.

  3. (c)

    Write e0=β^0−βe_{0}=\widehat{\beta}_{0}-\beta and β^λ=β^0+λ​v+λ2​w+OL2​(λ3)\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}=\widehat{\beta}_{0}+\lambda v+\lambda^{2}w+O_{L^{2}}(\lambda^{3}), with integrable loss remainders. Then the linear risk coefficient is 2​𝔼​⟨e0,v⟩2\mathbb{E}\langle e_{0},v\rangle and the quadratic coefficient is 𝔼​‖v‖2+2​𝔼​⟨e0,w⟩\mathbb{E}\|v\|^{2}+2\mathbb{E}\langle e_{0},w\rangle. If ∥e0∥L2=O(n−1/2)\|e_{0}\|_{L^{2}}=O(n^{-1/2}), ∥v∥L2=O(γnn−1/2)\|v\|_{L^{2}}=O(\gamma_{n}n^{-1/2}) and ∥w∥L2=O(γn2n−1/2)\|w\|_{L^{2}}=O(\gamma_{n}^{2}n^{-1/2}), these coefficients are bounded by O⁡(γn/n)O(\gamma_{n}/n) and O⁡(γn2/n)O(\gamma_{n}^{2}/n), respectively.

The rate bounds locate the finite-sample effects generated by the auxiliary Jacobian and covariance update. Their signed coefficients are examined through the exact conditional-risk identities in the main paper. Section 5.4.1 provides a convergent approximation with an explicit remainder, and Supplementary Section S2.12 gives the rate argument.

S2.2 Target and strength parameterization

The decomposition in the main paper identifies what a family member actually chooses. The first term of (53) is the prediction-corrected channel, and its metric W11W_{11} is determined by the selected weight; the second term is a penalty on the auxiliary moment whose metric ΠW\Pi_{W} changes with the weight. In the corrected basis of Section 5.2, therefore, a frozen criterion is determined by its auxiliary residual metric together with the strength, and both are read off from the covariance target of Section 3.3.

To make this correspondence explicit, write an nn-scaled target as S∗=𝖲+T​K​T⊤S_{*}=\mathsf{S}+TKT^{\top}, where 𝖲=S^/c1,n\mathsf{S}=\widehat{S}/c_{1,n} with K=K⊤K=K^{\top} symmetric, so that in the family’s notation the blended covariance is

𝖲λ,K=(1−λ)​𝖲+λ​S∗=𝖲+λ​T​K​T⊤.\mathsf{S}_{\lambda,K}=(1-\lambda)\mathsf{S}+\lambda S_{*}=\mathsf{S}+\lambda TKT^{\top}. (S2.1)

Because Bc​T=(0,−I)⊤B_{c}T=(0,-I)^{\top} in the notation of (58), such a target preserves the first block row (Vc,Rc)(V_{c},R_{c}) for every symmetric KK, and by Proposition 5.1 every target with that property has this form with Ω+K≻0\Omega+K\succ 0. Substituting S∗S_{*} into the corrected-basis criterion (60) gives

QK​(θ)=c​(θ)⊤​Vc−1​c​(θ)+rc​(θ)⊤​(Ω+K)−1​rc​(θ),rc=m2−Rc⊤​Vc−1​c.Q_{K}(\theta)=c(\theta)^{\top}V_{c}^{-1}c(\theta)+r_{c}(\theta)^{\top}(\Omega+K)^{-1}r_{c}(\theta),\qquad r_{c}=m_{2}-R_{c}^{\top}V_{c}^{-1}c. (S2.2)

The displayed criterion is the full-target endpoint. At strength λ\lambda, its residual metric is Ω+λ​K\Omega+\lambda K, while the corrected-channel term stays fixed. Thus the pair (Ω+K,λ)(\Omega+K,\lambda) determines the member, the target index α\alpha acting through the residual metric M=Ω+KM=\Omega+K in the parameterization of Proposition 5.1. Because Bc​T​K​T⊤​Bc⊤=diag⁡(0,K)B_{c}TKT^{\top}B_{c}^{\top}=\operatorname{diag}(0,K), membership in that class is exactly the requirement that the update be of the form T​K​T⊤TKT^{\top} for a symmetric KK; the calibrated target of Subsection 5.2 is constructed in this form, and so is the original covariance 𝖲\mathsf{S} itself, which corresponds to K=0K=0. The other targets of Supplementary Section S1.1 generally fall outside this class: their updates can change the first block row (Vc,Rc)(V_{c},R_{c}) of the corrected basis. Those targets therefore define different estimation problems rather than members of the calibrated class, and they are used below only as comparators. The finite-sample problem of this section is the choice of the pair (M,λ)(M,\lambda) within the calibrated class; Subsection 5.2 fixes MM and Supplementary Section S4.2 then determines λ\lambda.

S2.3 The implemented calibrated target

The covariance-calibrated PPI (CC-PPI) was defined in Section 3.4 by the target (27) and the estimator (25). In the corrected basis of (58), S0,ncal=c1,n​(𝖲+T​Kp​T⊤)S_{0,n}^{\rm cal}=c_{1,n}(\mathsf{S}+TK_{p}T^{\top}) is the additive form of (S2.1) with S0,n=S0,ncalS_{0,n}=S_{0,n}^{\rm cal}, and the pair of Supplementary Section S2.2 is the residual metric M=Ω+KpM=\Omega+K_{p} together with λ\lambda. The implemented CC-PPI estimator uses the default h=1/2h=1/2 of (24); the analysis varies λ\lambda over the protected path, and Supplementary Section S4.2 determines what that default costs relative to the best strength on the same path. The nn-scaled path (S2.5) used for the risk calculations records the same estimator, since multiplication of a covariance by a positive scalar leaves the GMM minimizer unchanged.

Two properties follow from this definition. First, Δp\Delta_{p} is by definition a symmetric update of the form T​K​T⊤TKT^{\top}, so S0,ncalS_{0,n}^{\rm cal} preserves the corrected channel by Proposition 5.1, and its criterion is exactly (60) with K=KpK=K_{p}. Second, the clipping is performed in the whitened coordinates in which the guarantee is expressed, (S2.3) below; a clip applied entrywise to F1/2​(CU−CL)​F1/2F^{1/2}(C_{U}-C_{L})F^{1/2} would not bound its spectrum, whereas clipping its eigenvalues makes 𝖲−1/2Δp𝖲−1/2\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}\Delta_{p}\mathsf{S}^{-1/2} have rank at most dd and spectrum inside [−κ,κ][-\kappa,\kappa], ensuring positive definiteness throughout the path. Under the covariance consistency conditions, the weight perturbation also vanishes in the regular limit.

S2.4 Protection and the common efficient path

The protection is the one announced in (27): it uses the whitened coordinates of the current covariance.

Ep\displaystyle E_{p} =clip[−κ,κ](𝖲−1/2Δ𝖲−1/2),0<κ<1,\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}_{[-\kappa,\kappa]}(\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}\Delta\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}),\quad 0<\kappa<1, (S2.3)

Here clipping acts on symmetric eigenvalues, and is performed once before varying strength. The target subscript 0,n0,n follows Section 3; it does not denote the endpoint λ=0\lambda=0. We use κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 and the default h=1/2h=1/2.

Protection preserves the calibration class. Indeed, with F=T⊤​𝖲−1​T≻0F=T^{\top}\mathsf{S}^{-1}T\succ 0,

Δp=TKpT⊤,Kp=F−1/2clip[−κ,κ](F1/2KF1/2)F−1/2.\Delta_{p}=TK_{p}T^{\top},\qquad K_{p}=F^{-1/2}\operatorname{clip}_{[-\kappa,\kappa]}(F^{1/2}KF^{1/2})F^{-1/2}. (S2.6)

To verify this, 𝖲−1/2TF−1/2\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}TF^{-1/2} has orthonormal columns, and the clipping function vanishes at zero. The nonzero spectral update stays on that subspace. The resulting criterion is (63) in the main paper.

If Kp⪰0K_{p}\succeq 0, increasing strength weakens this residual penalty; if Kp⪯0K_{p}\preceq 0, it strengthens it. Indefinite corrections have no uniform ordering. These are objective statements, not MSE statements. The residual root, when it exists, need not coincide with the root of m2m_{2}.

Within the linear, congruence-equivariant pooling family, Proposition S2.6 gives F=(1−ξ)​CL+ξ​CUF=(1-\xi)C_{L}+\xi C_{U}. CC-PPI takes the unlabeled pool F=CUF=C_{U}, directing the calibration toward the additional covariance information while retaining the corrected channel.

Under the covariance consistency conditions of Section 4.1, both CLC_{L} and CUC_{U} converge to Σh​h\Sigma_{hh}. At a regular positive definite limit, (S2.3) is continuous and Δp→p0\Delta_{p}\to_{p}0. This gives (64) in the main paper.

Corollary 4.3 applies to half strength and to bounded data-dependent selections on this path. A nonvanishing strength therefore need not sacrifice efficiency: the target perturbation itself vanishes. This statement excludes singular limiting covariances.

(i) ∥𝖲−1/2TKT⊤𝖲−1/2∥op=γK\|\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}TKT^{\top}\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}=\gamma_{K}. (ii) The reachable set of targets at relative amplitude at most one is {𝖲+TKT⊤:γK≤1,Ω+K≻0}\{\mathsf{S}+TKT^{\top}:\gamma_{K}\leq 1,\ \Omega+K\succ 0\}. (iii) For every λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1],

The strength and cap therefore control the same amplitude: the strength λ\lambda and the cap κ\kappa enter the sandwich (S2.8) only through the product λ​γK\lambda\gamma_{K}, so (λ,κ)=(1/2,1/2)(\lambda,\kappa)=(1/2,1/2) and (λ,κ)=(1,1/4)(\lambda,\kappa)=(1,1/4) carry the same amplitude bound. The cap guarantees admissibility.

Proposition S2.3 (Admissible caps).

(i) For every 0<κ<10<\kappa<1, every λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] and every symmetric KK with γK≤κ\gamma_{K}\leq\kappa, the blend 𝖲+λ​T​K​T⊤\mathsf{S}+\lambda TKT^{\top} is positive definite. (ii) For the two-parameter family K⁡(a,b)=a​Kp+b​γ​ΩK(a,b)=aK_{p}+b\gamma\Omega, |a|+|b|≤1|a|+|b|\leq 1, with γ=γKp\gamma=\gamma_{K_{p}}, positive definiteness follows from 1+b​γ>|a|​γ1+b\gamma>|a|\gamma; this holds for every admissible (a,b)(a,b) whenever γ<1/(|a|+|b|)\gamma<1/(|a|+|b|), and it fails at (a,b)=(1/2,−1/2)(a,b)=(1/2,-1/2) when γ=1\gamma=1 and the negative extremal direction is attained.

Part (i) gives the positive-definiteness guarantee provided by the cap: it delivers the invariant γ≤κ\gamma\leq\kappa of (S2.3) and hence positive definiteness along the whole path at every strength, and at the default strength h=1/2h=1/2 with κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 it gives the relative interval [3/4,5/4][3/4,5/4] in (S2.8). Part (ii) shows the role of the strict amplitude bound: at unit amplitude the borderline combination of the calibrated and isotropic directions leaves the class. No optimality of κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 is claimed; any cap strictly below one gives the positive-definiteness guarantee in part (i).

What the class cannot see is also part of its design. The residual metric enters the criterion only through its compression to the span of the realized residual values.

Proposition S2.4 (Only the realized residual span matters).

Let rc:Θ→ℝdr_{c}:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be arbitrary, put V=span⁡{rc​(θ):θ∈Θ}V=\operatorname{span}\{r_{c}(\theta):\theta\in\Theta\}, and let Π\Pi be the orthogonal projector onto VV. Then for every symmetric positive definite MM and every θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta,

rc​(θ)⊤​M−1​rc​(θ)=rc​(θ)⊤​Π​M−1​Π​rc​(θ).r_{c}(\theta)^{\top}M^{-1}r_{c}(\theta)=r_{c}(\theta)^{\top}\Pi M^{-1}\Pi\,r_{c}(\theta). (S2.9)

For affine rc​(θ)=J​θ−jr_{c}(\theta)=J\theta-j with full-dimensional Θ\Theta the converse holds; if the realized residual set is thin the criteria can agree while the compressions differ.

We next examine the local risk effect of an update in this class. The following statement is local in strength and applies to arbitrary smooth moments. In the affine class of (54), its local coefficients follow from the exact path analyzed below.

The first-order risk alignment is linear in the update, whereas the acceleration term is quadratic. Both contribute to the local response in (S2.11). The exact signed identity in the main paper retains the complete dependence induced by the data-based calibration; Supplementary Section S2.15 also gives an independent centered-update example illustrating the acceleration contribution.

S2.6 The calibration as a quadratic score-covariance map

The target has a concrete moment interpretation in regression. For each sample, put Bi=xi​xi⊤−ADB_{i}=x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}-A_{D} and ai=xi​fi−x​f¯Da_{i}=x_{i}f_{i}-\overline{xf}_{D}, where D=L,UD=L,U. Then

CD​(t)=aveD⁡{(Bi​t−ai)​(Bi​t−ai)⊤}.C_{D}(t)=\operatorname{ave}_{D}\{(B_{i}t-a_{i})(B_{i}t-a_{i})^{\top}\}. (S2.12)

Thus CU−CLC_{U}-C_{L} depends on fourth-order design moments, prediction-weighted cross moments and prediction-score second moments, through a quadratic function of tt. Matching covariate means and covariances alone, or knowing prediction MSE alone, does not establish the favorable sign in Theorem 5.3. The sign is in fact design-dependent rather than automatic: the same three-point calculation yields both the favorable regime p+u<1p+u<1 and the adverse regime p+u>1p+u>1 of Theorem 5.4. The theorem establishes a favorable region with a quantified tolerance. Broader design conditions beyond the three-point model and its local perturbations remain to be derived.

Expanding the first term of (53) gives cross term 2​m1⊤​W12​m22m_{1}^{\top}W_{12}m_{2} and lower term m2⊤​W21​W11−1​W12​m2m_{2}^{\top}W_{21}\allowbreak W_{11}^{-1}W_{12}m_{2}. Adding the Schur complement restores m2⊤​W22​m2m_{2}^{\top}W_{22}m_{2}. Positive definiteness of WW implies W11≻0W_{11}\succ 0 and ΠW≻0\Pi_{W}\succ 0. For m2=A5​θ−b2m_{2}=A_{5}\theta-b_{2}, its quadratic coefficient is A5⊤​ΠW​A5A_{5}^{\top}\Pi_{W}A_{5}. The Hessian of that term is twice this coefficient. No inverse of A5A_{5} is used unless an anchor root is explicitly defined.

An invertible simultaneous transformation of moments and covariance leaves the criterion invariant. In the corrected basis, channel preservation makes the symmetric difference diag⁡(0,K)\operatorname{diag}(0,K). Since Bc​T=(0,−I)⊤B_{c}T=(0,-I)^{\top}, transformation back proves uniqueness of T​K​T⊤TKT^{\top}. The factorization

(VcRcRc⊤Dc+K)=(I0Rc⊤​Vc−1I)​diag⁡(Vc,Ω+K)​(IVc−1​Rc0I)\begin{pmatrix}V_{c}&R_{c}\\ R_{c}^{\top}&D_{c}+K\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\ R_{c}^{\top}V_{c}^{-1}&I\end{pmatrix}\operatorname{diag}(V_{c},\Omega+K)\begin{pmatrix}I&V_{c}^{-1}R_{c}\\ 0&I\end{pmatrix} (S2.13)

proves both the definiteness test and (60). Along the protected path, only (Ω+λ​Kp)−1(\Omega+\lambda K_{p})^{-1} changes. Its derivative is −(Ω+λ​Kp)−1​Kp​(Ω+λ​Kp)−1-(\Omega+\lambda K_{p})^{-1}K_{p}(\Omega+\lambda K_{p})^{-1}, establishing the stated ordering for positive or negative corrections. This ordering alone does not order the minimizers’ MSEs.

S2.8 Pooling characterization and its boundaries

Proposition S2.6 (Pooling characterization).

If a raw pool ℱ⁡(A,D)\mathcal{F}(A,D) is linear on pairs of symmetric matrices, equivariant under all invertible congruences, positive definite for positive definite inputs, and satisfies ℱ⁡(A,A)=A\mathcal{F}(A,A)=A, then

ℱ⁡(A,D)=(1−λ)​A+λ​D,λ∈[0,1].\mathcal{F}(A,D)=(1-\lambda)A+\lambda D,\qquad\lambda\in[0,1]. (S2.14)
Proof.

Write a linear pool as ℱ⁡(A,D)=ℒ1​(A)+ℒ2​(D)\mathcal{F}(A,D)=\mathcal{L}_{1}(A)+\mathcal{L}_{2}(D). Each component is congruence-equivariant by setting the other input to zero in the equivariance identity. For d≥2d\geq 2, let E11=e1​e1⊤E_{11}=e_{1}e_{1}^{\top} and Qt=diag⁡(1,t​Id−1)Q_{t}=\operatorname{diag}(1,tI_{d-1}). Because Qt​E11​Qt⊤=E11Q_{t}E_{11}Q_{t}^{\top}=E_{11} for every t>0t>0, invariance forces the off-diagonal and lower blocks of ℒj​(E11)\mathcal{L}_{j}(E_{11}) to vanish. Thus ℒj​(E11)=aj​E11\mathcal{L}_{j}(E_{11})=a_{j}E_{11}. For d=1d=1, every linear component already has the scalar form ℒj​(A)=aj​A\mathcal{L}_{j}(A)=a_{j}A. For d≥2d\geq 2 and any nonzero xx, choose an invertible QQ with Q​e1=xQe_{1}=x. Equivariance gives ℒj​(x​x⊤)=aj​x​x⊤\mathcal{L}_{j}(xx^{\top})=a_{j}xx^{\top}. Rank-one spectral decompositions and linearity yield ℒj​(A)=aj​A\mathcal{L}_{j}(A)=a_{j}A for every symmetric AA; the coefficients do not depend on the argument values. The common-input condition gives a1+a2=1a_{1}+a_{2}=1. It remains to exclude a negative coefficient, as follows. Suppose instead that a1<0a_{1}<0, so a2=1−a1>1>0a_{2}=1-a_{1}>1>0; fix any A≻0A\succ 0 and set D=−(a1/a2)​AD=-(a_{1}/a_{2})A, which is positive definite because −a1/a2>0-a_{1}/a_{2}>0. Then ℱ⁡(A,D)=a1​A+a2​D=0\mathcal{F}(A,D)=a_{1}A+a_{2}D=0, contradicting the positivity axiom. Hence a1≥0a_{1}\geq 0, and exchanging the roles gives a2≥0a_{2}\geq 0. With a1+a2=1a_{1}+a_{2}=1 both coefficients lie in [0,1][0,1], so λ:=a2\lambda:=a_{2} satisfies ℱ⁡(A,D)=(1−λ)​A+λ​D\mathcal{F}(A,D)=(1-\lambda)A+\lambda D. The converse follows directly. ∎

These assumptions constrain the construction, not all uses of the available information. The characterization is sharp: the harmonic pool 2​(A−1+D−1)−12(A^{-1}+D^{-1})^{-1} is positive, congruence-equivariant and common-input consistent, but nonlinear. For A=diag⁡(1,4)A=\operatorname{diag}(1,4) and D=diag⁡(4,1)D=\operatorname{diag}(4,1) it equals diag⁡(1.6,1.6)\operatorname{diag}(1.6,1.6), requiring different scalar mixture coefficients in the two coordinates. It nevertheless remains in the same residual mechanism if it is inserted through Proposition 5.1 and the resulting covariance is positive definite.

If targets share one protected update, Sj=𝖲+λj​ΔpS_{j}=\mathsf{S}+\lambda_{j}\Delta_{p}, any convex average is 𝖲+(∑jwj​λj)​Δp\mathsf{S}+(\sum_{j}w_{j}\lambda_{j})\Delta_{p}. Separately protecting scaled raw targets need not have this property: eigenvalue clipping is nonlinear. Structural equivalence, equality of covariance paths, and equality of estimates are therefore distinct.

S2.9 Protection, convergence, and its exact support

Let F=T⊤​𝖲−1​TF=T^{\top}\mathsf{S}^{-1}T and QT=𝖲−1/2TF−1/2Q_{T}=\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}TF^{-1/2}. Then QT⊤​QT=IQ_{T}^{\top}Q_{T}=I and

𝖲−1/2TKT⊤𝖲−1/2=QT(F1/2KF1/2)QT⊤.\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}TKT^{\top}\mathsf{S}^{-1/2}=Q_{T}(F^{1/2}KF^{1/2})Q_{T}^{\top}. (S2.15)

The orthogonal complement has eigenvalue zero. Applying a spectral function that vanishes at zero and transforming back proves (S2.6). In particular rank⁡(Δp)≤d\operatorname{rank}(\Delta_{p})\leq d and channel preservation survives active clipping. Since −κ​I⪯Ep⪯κ​I-\kappa I\preceq E_{p}\preceq\kappa I,

(1−λ​κ)​𝖲⪯𝖲+λ​Δp⪯(1+λ​κ)​𝖲.(1-\lambda\kappa)\mathsf{S}\preceq\mathsf{S}+\lambda\Delta_{p}\preceq(1+\lambda\kappa)\mathsf{S}. (S2.16)

At λ=1/2\lambda=1/2, κ=1/2\kappa=1/2, the relative covariance interval is [3/4,5/4][3/4,5/4] and the relative inverse interval is [4/5,4/3][4/5,4/3].

Under the pilot uniform laws of Supplementary Section S1, CL−CU→p0C_{L}-C_{U}\to_{p}0. The regular limit 𝖲→pS/c1≻0\mathsf{S}\to_{p}S/c_{1}\succ 0 makes square roots, inverse square roots and clipping continuous there. Consequently Δp→p0\Delta_{p}\to_{p}0. S2.10 Growth, weak derivatives, and Gaussian integrability

Here the design, prediction values, sample sizes and positive ridge are fixed. Put Sλ=𝖲+λ​ΔpS_{\lambda}=\mathsf{S}+\lambda\Delta_{p} and b=b⁡(Y)b=b(Y). Score vectors are affine in YY through t=C​Yt=CY, so for fixed constants cic_{i},

‖𝖲⁡(Y)‖≤c0​(1+‖Y‖2),‖b⁡(Y)‖≤c1​(1+‖Y‖),λmin​(Sλ)≥(1−κ)​η.\|\mathsf{S}(Y)\|\leq c_{0}(1+\|Y\|^{2}),\quad\|b(Y)\|\leq c_{1}(1+\|Y\|),\quad\lambda_{\min}(S_{\lambda})\geq(1-\kappa)\eta. (S2.17)

For Gλ=Sλ−1/2HG_{\lambda}=S_{\lambda}^{-1/2}H, the smallest singular value is at least smin​(H)/‖Sλ‖s_{\min}(H)/\sqrt{\|S_{\lambda}\|}. The least-squares pseudoinverse formula therefore gives

‖β^λ‖≤(1+κ)/(1−κ)smin​(H)​‖𝖲‖/η​‖b‖≤c2​(1+‖Y‖2),\|\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}\|\leq\frac{\sqrt{(1+\kappa)/(1-\kappa)}}{s_{\min}(H)}\sqrt{\|\mathsf{S}\|/\eta}\,\|b\|\leq c_{2}(1+\|Y\|^{2}), (S2.18)

uniformly in strength. Finite fourth moments of the errors suffice for square-integrable fits and hence Theorem 5.3. They alone do not establish the derivative moment conditions used in the Gaussian results.

For completeness, symmetric clipping is the Frobenius projection onto the closed convex set {A=A⊤:−κ​I⪯A⪯κ​I}\{A=A^{\top}:-\kappa I\preceq A\preceq\kappa I\}. Diagonalize the input: the projection inequality follows coordinatewise from scalar clipping and the bounds on the diagonal entries of every feasible comparison matrix. Applying this inequality to two projected inputs shows that the projection is nonexpansive. Thus clipping is Lipschitz, including at eigenvalue coincidences and thresholds.

For S⪰η​IS\succeq\eta I, the differential Z=D​(S1/2)​[D​S]Z=D(S^{1/2})[DS] solves S1/2​Z+Z​S1/2=D​SS^{1/2}Z+ZS^{1/2}=DS. In an eigenbasis,

Zi​j=(D​S)i​j/(si+sj),‖Z‖F≤‖D​S‖F/(2​η).Z_{ij}=(DS)_{ij}/(\sqrt{s_{i}}+\sqrt{s_{j}}),\qquad\|Z\|_{F}\leq\|DS\|_{F}/(2\sqrt{\eta}). (S2.19)

Inverse-root derivatives follow by differentiating the inverse. Combining these bounds with polynomial score derivatives proves local Lipschitzness and polynomial-growth weak derivative bounds for Ep,Δp,Sλ−1E_{p},\Delta_{p},S_{\lambda}^{-1}. Furthermore λmin​(H⊤​Sλ−1​H)≥smin​(H)2/‖Sλ‖\lambda_{\min}(H^{\top}S_{\lambda}^{-1}H)\geq s_{\min}(H)^{2}/\|S_{\lambda}\|, so its inverse and derivatives have polynomial bounds too. The actual fit and vλ=∂λβ^λv_{\lambda}=\partial_{\lambda}\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda} consequently have first weak response derivatives with polynomial-growth bounds, uniformly in λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]. Gaussian responses have all polynomial moments. This proves the required integrability and interchanges below for the implemented fixed-design pipeline. Constants can depend badly on the design and ridge; no useful uniform-in-nn rate is asserted.

S2.11 The raw covariance correction as a quadratic polynomial

Centering xi​xi⊤​t−xi​fix_{i}x_{i}^{\top}t-x_{i}f_{i} gives Bi​t−aiB_{i}t-a_{i} as defined in (S2.12). For a unit vector ww, put

Proposition S2.1 is a random-design statement. In affine regression, the coefficients of m2​(θ)m_{2}(\theta) are the differences of sample averages of X​X⊤XX^{\top} and X​f​(X)Xf(X). Appendix S3 Risk Transfer and Same-Data Selection

S3.1 Conditional projection refinements

Under ϵ∼N⁡(0,σ2​I)\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}I), r=(I−X​C)​Yr=(I-XC)Y is independent of tt. Conditional projections given rr yield the same theorem with all projection coefficients computed conditionally and then averaged over rr. Write Qgcond=𝔼​‖g−ag​(r)−Ag​(r)​z‖2Q_{g}^{\rm cond}=\mathbb{E}\|g-a_{g}(r)-A_{g}(r)z\|^{2} and Qucond=𝔼​‖u−au​(r)−Au​(r)​z‖2Q_{u}^{\rm cond}=\mathbb{E}\|u-a_{u}(r)-A_{u}(r)z\|^{2} for these conditional residual energies, distinct from the unconditional Qg,QuQ_{g},Q_{u} in the main paper. For square-integrable first weak derivatives,

Qgcond≤12​{𝔼​‖Dz​g‖F2−𝔼r​‖Ag​(r)‖F2},Qucond≤12​{𝔼​‖Dz​u‖F2−𝔼r​‖Au​(r)‖F2}.Q_{g}^{\rm cond}\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\{\mathbb{E}\|D_{z}g\|_{F}^{2}-\mathbb{E}_{r}\|A_{g}(r)\|_{F}^{2}\},\quad Q_{u}^{\rm cond}\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\{\mathbb{E}\|D_{z}u\|_{F}^{2}-\mathbb{E}_{r}\|A_{u}(r)\|_{F}^{2}\}. (S3.1)

To see this, expand in normalized Gaussian Hermite polynomials conditional on rr. After removing degrees zero and one, all remaining degrees are at least two; Parseval and the derivative identity charge their energy at least twice in the Gaussian Dirichlet form. Averaging gives (S3.1). The positive ridge and Lipschitz spectral clipping allow weak first derivatives with polynomial growth, although classical second derivatives may fail at clipping thresholds. These derivatives include every pilot, covariance and protection operation. The weak-derivative Stein framework in (Bellec and Zhang, 2021) is useful here.

S3.2 Proof of the midpoint minimax-regret proposition

Proof.

The map ζ↦(λ−ζ)2\zeta\mapsto(\lambda-\zeta)^{2} is convex, so its supremum over an interval is attained at an endpoint; this gives (73). Both branches are convex and nonnegative, so their maximum is convex; it is invariant under the reflection λ↦l+u−λ\lambda\mapsto l+u-\lambda that exchanges the branches, strictly decreasing below (l+u)/2(l+u)/2 and strictly increasing above it, so the minimum is unique at (l+u)/2(l+u)/2 and equals B​((u−l)/2)2B((u-l)/2)^{2}. For the prior statement, expand (λ−ζ)2=(λ−m)2+2​(λ−m)​(m−ζ)+(ζ−m)2(\lambda-\zeta)^{2}=(\lambda-m)^{2}+2(\lambda-m)(m-\zeta)+(\zeta-m)^{2}; the cross term has zero π\pi-expectation and the last has expectation AπA_{\pi}. ∎

For every fixed λ\lambda, its expectation is R⁡(λ)−R⁡(h)R(\lambda)-R(h). Zλ=∂λeλ\displaystyle Z_{\lambda}=\partial_{\lambda}e_{\lambda} =−2​{ϵ⊤​C⊤​vλ−σ2​tr⁡[(DY​vλ)​C⊤]},\displaystyle=-2\{\epsilon^{\top}C^{\top}v_{\lambda}-\sigma^{2}\operatorname{tr}[(D_{Y}v_{\lambda})C^{\top}]\}, (S3.3)

Let a finite grid 𝒢⊂[0,1]\mathcal{G}\subset[0,1] contain hh, with the grid and τ>0\tau>0 deterministic conditional on the designs, and assume ℬ<∞\mathcal{B}<\infty. The selector

λ^τ∈arg⁡minλ∈𝒢​{q^λ+τ​|λ−h|}\widehat{\lambda}_{\tau}\in\arg\min_{\lambda\in\mathcal{G}}\{\widehat{q}_{\lambda}+\tau|\lambda-h|\} (S3.5)

satisfies

This controls possible deterioration; it is not a lower bound on selection cost or a theorem that tuning is harmful. For unknown noise variance, a plug-in σ^2\widehat{\sigma}^{2} adds 2​(σ^2−σ2)​⟨C,DY​(β^λ−β^h)⟩F2(\widehat{\sigma}^{2}-\sigma^{2})\langle C,D_{Y}(\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\widehat{\beta}_{h})\rangle_{F} to the criterion error. Its joint moments with the learned maps must be retained; the unbiased fixed-candidate argument cannot be reused unchanged. Numerical derivative error likewise needs an explicit allowance. In an eight-law, 64-design validation with d=2,5d=2,5, n=40,160n=40,160, N=5​nN=5n, and two predictor discrepancies, direct known-noise parameter-SURE selection had higher average risk than half in four laws and lower risk in four. The paired differences were small relative to the design-level Monte Carlo errors. In this comparison, response-based selection gave no consistent improvement over the fixed half-strength rule.

Numerical evaluation of the primitive improvement regime.

The numerical example n=40n=40, N=200N=200, a=σ=1a=\sigma=1, p=0.4p=0.4, u=0.2u=0.2 has numerically integrated 𝒢ref≃9.3800×10−4\mathcal{G}_{\rm ref}\simeq 9.3800\times 10^{-4}. At μ=0.0625\mu=0.0625, (71) is approximately 2.9436×10−42.9436\times 10^{-4}, leaving a positive lower margin of approximately 6.4364×10−46.4364\times 10^{-4}; the integrated actual gain is approximately 9.0054×10−49.0054\times 10^{-4}. These are quadrature evaluations of a proved inequality, not certified integration bounds. Supplementary Section S3.5 additionally gives a conservative analytic lower margin and moment upper bounds that establish a nonempty tolerance range without numerical integration. Stability under small design or prediction perturbations is established in Supplementary Section S3.7; no uniform or high-dimensional radius is asserted.

S3.6 Gaussian-shift transfer in every fixed dimension

Let the fixed external predictor be f⁡(x)=x⊤​αf(x)=x^{\top}\alpha, μ=β−α\mu=\beta-\alpha, Vt=σ2​(X⊤​X)−1V_{t}=\sigma^{2}(X^{\top}X)^{-1} and v=t−αv=t-\alpha. Under Gaussian errors, v∼N⁡(μ,Vt)v\sim N(\mu,V_{t}) independently of r=(I−X​C)​Yr=(I-XC)Y. Write the actual fit as β^λ=α+aλ​(v,r)\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}=\alpha+a_{\lambda}(v,r). Its centered affine moments have right-hand side (AL​v,0)⊤(A_{L}v,0)^{\top}. Joint reflection (v,r)↦(−v,−r)(v,r)\mapsto(-v,-r) changes the sign of all pilot scores, preserves their centered covariance, ridge and protected update, and changes the sign of this right-hand side. Consequently aλ​(−v,−r)=−aλ​(v,r)a_{\lambda}(-v,-r)=-a_{\lambda}(v,r).

For deterministic strengths s,bs,b, define hs​b=‖as‖2−‖ab‖2h_{sb}=\|a_{s}\|^{2}-\|a_{b}\|^{2}, js​b=as−abj_{sb}=a_{s}-a_{b}, Hs​b=‖hs​b‖L2​(ℙ0)H_{sb}=\|h_{sb}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{P}_{0})} and Js​b=‖js​b‖L2​(ℙ0)J_{sb}=\|j_{sb}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{P}_{0})}. The maps are evaluated under the zero-shift reference law ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{0}; they contain no unknown β\beta argument. Put qμ=μ⊤​Vt−1​μq_{\mu}=\mu^{\top}V_{t}^{-1}\mu. The likelihood ratio is ℓμ​(v)=exp⁡(μ⊤​Vt−1​v−qμ/2)\ell_{\mu}(v)=\exp(\mu^{\top}V_{t}^{-1}v-q_{\mu}/2). Its reflection-even and reflection-odd parts satisfy

𝔼0​(ℓeven−1)2=cosh⁡(qμ)−1,𝔼0​ℓodd2=sinh⁡(qμ).\mathbb{E}_{0}(\ell_{\rm even}-1)^{2}=\cosh(q_{\mu})-1,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{0}\ell_{\rm odd}^{2}=\sinh(q_{\mu}). (S3.28)

Evenness of hs​bh_{sb} and oddness of js​bj_{sb} give

Rμ​(s)−Rμ​(b)=𝔼0​[hs​b​ℓeven]−2​μ⊤​𝔼0​[js​b​ℓodd].R_{\mu}(s)-R_{\mu}(b)=\mathbb{E}_{0}[h_{sb}\ell_{\rm even}]-2\mu^{\top}\mathbb{E}_{0}[j_{sb}\ell_{\rm odd}]. (S3.29)

Subtract the zero-shift contrast and apply Cauchy–Schwarz to obtain

|Rμ​(s)−Rμ​(b)−R0​(s)+R0​(b)|≤Hs​b​cosh⁡(qμ)−1+2​‖μ‖​Js​b​sinh⁡(qμ).|R_{\mu}(s)-R_{\mu}(b)-R_{0}(s)+R_{0}(b)|\leq H_{sb}\sqrt{\cosh(q_{\mu})-1}+2\|\mu\|J_{sb}\sqrt{\sinh(q_{\mu})}. (S3.30)

All moments are finite by the fixed-design Gaussian growth bounds. For a fixed design this perturbation is O⁡(‖μ‖2)O(\|\mu\|^{2}) near zero. Setting s=h,b=0s=h,b=0 proves the main theorem. In higher dimensions this transfers a reference gain when one is separately established; supplying a favorable reference sign for arbitrary designs remains open (Supplementary Section S5). No data-selected strength can be substituted without accounting for its selection map.

S3.7 Stability of an established improvement margin

Consider two fixed design/prediction configurations with the same n,N,d,β,σ,η>0n,N,d,\beta,\sigma,\eta>0 and cap, and couple their responses using the same standard Gaussian noise. Superscripts 0,10,1 distinguish their actual fitted maps. For a∈{0,h}a\in\{0,h\} put da=‖β^a1−β^a0‖L2d_{a}=\|\widehat{\beta}_{a}^{1}-\widehat{\beta}_{a}^{0}\|_{L^{2}}. The exact loss expansion and Cauchy–Schwarz give

|Ra1−Ra0|≤2​Ra0​da+da2.|R_{a}^{1}-R_{a}^{0}|\leq 2\sqrt{R_{a}^{0}}\,d_{a}+d_{a}^{2}. (S3.31)

Hence an established margin G0=R00−Rh0>0G^{0}=R_{0}^{0}-R_{h}^{0}>0 survives whenever

2​R00​d0+d02+2​Rh0​dh+dh2<G0.2\sqrt{R_{0}^{0}}\,d_{0}+d_{0}^{2}+2\sqrt{R_{h}^{0}}\,d_{h}+d_{h}^{2}<G^{0}. (S3.32)

At fixed positive ridge, the actual fit is continuous in finite design and prediction entries near any full-rank labeled design: the pilot, positive-definite square roots, spectral clipping and normal-equation inverses are continuous. On a sufficiently small compact neighborhood the labeled singular value is bounded below and the polynomial Gaussian growth envelope in Supplementary Section S2.10 is uniform. Dominated convergence therefore makes d0,dh→0d_{0},d_{h}\to 0 as the configuration converges. Every strictly favorable reference configuration has an open neighborhood of favorable configurations of the same dimension, including predictions not exactly linear on the observed rows. This proves existence of a neighborhood, not a useful uniform numerical radius, a change of dimension, or improvement after averaging over arbitrary random designs.

S3.8 Conditioning, Hermite tails, and affine residual budgets

For homoscedastic Gaussian errors, r=(I−X​C)​ϵr=(I-XC)\epsilon and t−β=C​ϵt-\beta=C\epsilon are jointly Gaussian with cross covariance zero, since C⁡(I−X​C)=0C(I-XC)=0 and X​CXC is an orthogonal projector. They are independent. Given rr, z∼N⁡(0,Id)z\sim N(0,I_{d}). Use conditional coefficients ag​(r),Ag​(r),au​(r),Au​(r)a_{g}(r),A_{g}(r),a_{u}(r),A_{u}(r) and conditional projection residuals; then all preceding identities hold after averaging over rr. The resulting tail energies are Qgcond,QucondQ_{g}^{\rm cond},Q_{u}^{\rm cond} of (S3.1); the unconditional tails also include variation of the conditional affine coefficients.

Let {Hα}\{H_{\alpha}\} be normalized multivariate Hermite polynomials for standard Gaussian measure, indexed by multi-indices α∈ℕd\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{d}, with coefficients aα​(r)=𝔼z​[g​Hα​(z)∣r]a_{\alpha}(r)=\mathbb{E}_{z}[gH_{\alpha}(z)\mid r]. Orthogonality, completeness, and ∂jHα=αj​Hα−ej\partial_{j}H_{\alpha}=\sqrt{\alpha_{j}}H_{\alpha-e_{j}} imply, for vector-valued Gaussian Sobolev functions,

𝔼z​‖g‖2=∑α‖aα​(r)‖2,𝔼z​‖Dz​g‖F2=∑α|α|​‖aα​(r)‖2.\mathbb{E}_{z}\|g\|^{2}=\sum_{\alpha}\|a_{\alpha}(r)\|^{2},\qquad\mathbb{E}_{z}\|D_{z}g\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{\alpha}|\alpha|\|a_{\alpha}(r)\|^{2}. (S3.33)

For polynomials this follows term by term; for square-integrable weak derivatives it follows by completion in the Gaussian Sobolev norm. Degrees zero and one are precisely the affine projection, with degree-one coefficient matrix Ag​(r)A_{g}(r). Every remaining degree contributes at least twice its energy in the second identity. This proves (S3.1), including its factor 1/21/2. The same calculation applies to uu. The weak-derivative Gaussian integration-by-parts framework is consistent with (Bellec and Zhang, 2021); this tail decomposition is derived here rather than attributed as a theorem about our target.

First-order Stein also gives Ag​(r)=𝔼z​[Dz​g∣r]A_{g}(r)=\mathbb{E}_{z}[D_{z}g\mid r] and Au​(r)=𝔼z​[Dz​u∣r]A_{u}(r)=\mathbb{E}_{z}[D_{z}u\mid r]. In coordinates, Dz​g=(Dt​β^0−I)​JD_{z}g=(D_{t}\widehat{\beta}_{0}-I)J, Dz​u=(Dt​β^h−Dt​β^0)​JD_{z}u=(D_{t}\widehat{\beta}_{h}-D_{t}\widehat{\beta}_{0})J, holding rr fixed. Perturbing YY by X​vXv changes tt by vv and leaves rr unchanged, so these derivatives retain the entire same-response pipeline.

For any conditional affine approximation a⁡(r)+A⁡(r)​za(r)+A(r)z, orthogonality gives

𝔼z​‖g−a−A​z‖2=𝔼z​‖g⟂‖2+‖ag​(r)−a‖2+‖Ag​(r)−A‖F2.\mathbb{E}_{z}\|g-a-Az\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{z}\|g_{\perp}\|^{2}+\|a_{g}(r)-a\|^{2}+\|A_{g}(r)-A\|_{F}^{2}. (S3.34)

Thus independently fitted affine residuals bound the exact tail in population. Finite validation averages need uncertainty control before they become confidence bounds. These coefficients are theoretical diagnostics depending on unknown β\beta, not an automatically feasible selector.

S3.9 Parameter SURE and its variance identity

Let gλ=β^λ−tg_{\lambda}=\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-t and Fλ=C⊤​gλF_{\lambda}=C^{\top}g_{\lambda}. Gaussian integration by parts gives

R⁡(λ)=σ2​tr⁡(C​C⊤)+𝔼⁡{‖gλ‖2+2​σ2​⟨C,DY​gλ⟩F}.R(\lambda)=\sigma^{2}\operatorname{tr}(CC^{\top})+\mathbb{E}\{\|g_{\lambda}\|^{2}+2\sigma^{2}\langle C,D_{Y}g_{\lambda}\rangle_{F}\}. (S3.35)

Subtracting the equation at hh proves unbiasedness of (S3.2). This is parameter loss, not prediction loss in the observation space. The subtraction cancels the derivative of tt.

Set wλ=β^λ−β^hw_{\lambda}=\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\widehat{\beta}_{h}. Expanding the two losses around tt gives exactly

eλ=−2​{ϵ⊤​C⊤​wλ−σ2​tr⁡[(DY​wλ)​C⊤]}.e_{\lambda}=-2\{\epsilon^{\top}C^{\top}w_{\lambda}-\sigma^{2}\operatorname{tr}[(D_{Y}w_{\lambda})C^{\top}]\}. (S3.36)

Differentiate in strength, with all covariance operations frozen in strength but not in response, to get (S3.3). For a vector map F⁡(Y)F(Y) with square-integrable weak derivative, the second-order Stein identity (Bellec and Zhang, 2021) is

𝔼​{ϵ⊤​F−σ2​div⁡F}2=σ2​𝔼​‖F‖2+σ4​𝔼​tr⁡[(DY​F)2].\mathbb{E}\{\epsilon^{\top}F-\sigma^{2}\operatorname{div}F\}^{2}=\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}\|F\|^{2}+\sigma^{4}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{tr}[(D_{Y}F)^{2}]. (S3.37)

Apply it to F=C⊤​vλF=C^{\top}v_{\lambda}. Cyclicity of trace gives the matrix-square trace in (S3.4). Its replacement by the Frobenius norm is valid because |tr⁡(A2)|≤‖A‖F2|\operatorname{tr}(A^{2})|\leq\|A\|_{F}^{2}. Supplementary Section S2.10 supplies the needed Gaussian moments and weak derivatives. No classical second response derivative of the spectral clipping map is needed.

S3.10 Detailed selection inequality

Because eh=0e_{h}=0 and the error path is absolutely continuous in strength,

|eλ|≤|λ−h|​A​(Y),A​(Y)2=∫01Zs​(Y)2​𝑑s,𝔼​A2=ℬ.|e_{\lambda}|\leq\sqrt{|\lambda-h|}\,A(Y),\qquad A(Y)^{2}=\int_{0}^{1}Z_{s}(Y)^{2}ds,\quad\mathbb{E}A^{2}=\mathcal{B}. (S3.38)

The finite-grid selector is measurable after a deterministic tie-breaking rule. Comparing its objective to hh and writing d=|λ^τ−h|d=|\widehat{\lambda}_{\tau}-h| gives dλ^τ≤−τ​d−eλ^τ≤−τ​d+d​A≤A2/(4​τ)d_{\widehat{\lambda}_{\tau}}\leq-\tau d-e_{\widehat{\lambda}_{\tau}}\leq-\tau d+\sqrt{d}A\leq A^{2}/(4\tau). This proves the default-relative bound. Comparison to any fixed s∈𝒢s\in\mathcal{G} instead gives

dλ^τ−ds≤τ​|s−h|−τ​d+es−eλ^τ.d_{\widehat{\lambda}_{\tau}}-d_{s}\leq\tau|s-h|-\tau d+e_{s}-e_{\widehat{\lambda}_{\tau}}. (S3.39)

Taking expectations, using 𝔼​es=0\mathbb{E}e_{s}=0 and completing the same square proves the second bound. There is no grid-cardinality factor because the common anchored path controls every candidate simultaneously. It does not prove that the bound is tight. At τ=0\tau=0, the same argument and d≤1/2d\leq 1/2 give Rsel≤mins∈𝒢⁡R⁡(s)+ℬ/2R_{\rm sel}\leq\min_{s\in\mathcal{G}}R(s)+\sqrt{\mathcal{B}/2}.

For a purely discrete path, let ordered grid points contain hh. Define Agrid2=∑j(esj+1−esj)2/(sj+1−sj)A_{\rm grid}^{2}=\sum_{j}(e_{s_{j+1}}-e_{s_{j}})^{2}/(s_{j+1}-s_{j}). Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz proves the same envelope at grid points. Each error increment has second moment given by (S3.37) with F=C⊤​(β^sj+1−β^sj)F=C^{\top}(\widehat{\beta}_{s_{j+1}}-\widehat{\beta}_{s_{j}}) and factor four. Thus the selection proof can also be formulated with the discrete expected budget. For a differentiable path it is at most ℬ\mathcal{B}.

S3.11 Unknown variance and numerical derivative error

For a response-based σ^2\widehat{\sigma}^{2}, define q~λ\widetilde{q}_{\lambda} by substitution in (S3.2). Its error is

e~λ\displaystyle\widetilde{e}_{\lambda} =eλ+2​(σ^2−σ2)​tr⁡[(DY​wλ)​C⊤],\displaystyle=e_{\lambda}+2(\widehat{\sigma}^{2}-\sigma^{2})\operatorname{tr}[(D_{Y}w_{\lambda})C^{\top}], (S3.40)
Z~λ\displaystyle\widetilde{Z}_{\lambda} =Zλ+2​(σ^2−σ2)​tr⁡[(DY​vλ)​C⊤].\displaystyle=Z_{\lambda}+2(\widehat{\sigma}^{2}-\sigma^{2})\operatorname{tr}[(D_{Y}v_{\lambda})C^{\top}]. (S3.41)

The plug-in is fixed with respect to strength, not independent of response. Its fixed-candidate mean error need not vanish. Nevertheless, the pointwise default comparison still proves

Rsel,plugin≤R⁡(h)+𝔼⁡{∫01Z~s2​𝑑s4​τ​(Y)}R_{\rm sel,plugin}\leq R(h)+\mathbb{E}\left\{\frac{\int_{0}^{1}\widetilde{Z}_{s}^{2}ds}{4\tau(Y)}\right\} (S3.42)

for any positive response-dependent penalty with the displayed expectation finite. For deterministic τ\tau, a valid variance budget is

𝔼​∫01Z~s2​𝑑s≤2​ℬ+8​∫01𝔼⁡{(σ^2−σ2)2​tr⁡[(DY​vs)​C⊤]2}​𝑑s.\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{1}\widetilde{Z}_{s}^{2}ds\leq 2\mathcal{B}+8\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}\{(\widehat{\sigma}^{2}-\sigma^{2})^{2}\operatorname{tr}[(D_{Y}v_{s})C^{\top}]^{2}\}ds. (S3.43)

These are joint expectations; factoring them without independence is invalid. With n>dn>d, the OLS estimate σ^2=‖r‖2/(n−d)\widehat{\sigma}^{2}=\|r\|^{2}/(n-d) is feasible. Polynomial bounds ensure finiteness for a constant positive penalty. For a penalty proportional to σ^2\widehat{\sigma}^{2}, n−d>2n-d>2 is a sufficient inverse-residual-moment condition at fixed design: the Gaussian residual radius has a chi-square distribution with n−dn-d degrees of freedom, and its inverse first moment is finite precisely above two. This does not restore the unbiased fixed-candidate oracle comparison.

Suppose an approximate derivative-based contrast is anchored at zero for hh and differs uniformly from the exact contrast by at most b⁡(Y)b(Y) on the grid. The objective comparisons then add 𝔼​b\mathbb{E}b to the default bound and 2​𝔼​b2\mathbb{E}b to the known-noise fixed-candidate bound. They add 𝔼​b\mathbb{E}b to (S3.42). For a fixed finite grid, almost-everywhere differentiability and an integrable difference-quotient envelope give 𝔼​b→0\mathbb{E}b\to 0 as a central-difference step tends to zero. Polynomial weak-derivative bounds above provide domination for the actual Gaussian pipeline. A numerical step-halving audit is a diagnostic, not proof that b=0b=0 at the chosen step.

Finally, ⟨C,DY​β^λ⟩F=∑j=1dDCj⊤​β^λ,j\langle C,D_{Y}\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}\rangle_{F}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}D_{C_{j}^{\top}}\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda,j}. Thus dd response perturbation directions suffice for the parameter divergence. Every perturbed response requires recomputing the pilot, covariance, protection and final fit. Treating the weight as response-constant here would differentiate a different estimator.

Specifically, let a grid include both endpoints with maximum spacing aa, assume |R′′|≤ℳ|R^{\prime\prime}|\leq\mathcal{M}, and let g^j\widehat{g}_{j} estimate gj=R⁡(h)−R⁡(λj)g_{j}=R(h)-R(\lambda_{j}). On any simultaneous event |g^j−gj|≤bj|\widehat{g}_{j}-g_{j}|\leq b_{j},

max⁡{0,maxj⁡(g^j−bj)}≤Gh≤maxj⁡(g^j+bj)+ℳ​a2/8.\max\{0,\max_{j}(\widehat{g}_{j}-b_{j})\}\leq G_{h}\leq\max_{j}(\widehat{g}_{j}+b_{j})+\mathcal{M}a^{2}/8. (S4.2)

S4.2 Strength stationarity and conditional regret results

The exact strength path distinguishes two optimization problems. For a fixed response, let ℒY​(λ)=‖β^λ−β‖2\mathcal{L}_{Y}(\lambda)=\|\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\beta\|^{2} denote realized loss. The risk R⁡(λ)=𝔼​ℒY​(λ)R(\lambda)=\mathbb{E}\mathcal{L}_{Y}(\lambda) instead averages the response-dependent coefficients of that path. A truth-assisted minimum of realized loss is not the best fixed strength for risk.

Proposition S4.1 (Realized-loss stationarity polynomial).

Fix the design, predictor and response, and put m=rank⁡(Ep)≤dm=\operatorname{rank}(E_{p})\leq d. The realized loss can be written ℒY=NY/BY2\mathcal{L}_{Y}=N_{Y}/B_{Y}^{2} with polynomials of degrees at most 2​m2m and mm, respectively, and BYB_{Y} nonzero on [0,1][0,1]. Define

gY​(λ)=NY′​(λ)​BY​(λ)−2​NY​(λ)​BY′​(λ).g_{Y}(\lambda)=N_{Y}^{\prime}(\lambda)B_{Y}(\lambda)-2N_{Y}(\lambda)B_{Y}^{\prime}(\lambda). (S4.3)

Then ℒY′=gY/BY3\mathcal{L}_{Y}^{\prime}=g_{Y}/B_{Y}^{3}, and deg⁡gY≤3​m−1\deg g_{Y}\leq 3m-1 for m≥1m\geq 1. Unless the derivative is identically zero, the minimum realized loss is attained among the endpoints and interior real roots:

min[0,1]ℒY=min{ℒY(0),ℒY(1),ℒY(λ):gY(λ)=0, 0<λ<1}.\min_{[0,1]}\mathcal{L}_{Y}=\min\{\mathcal{L}_{Y}(0),\mathcal{L}_{Y}(1),\mathcal{L}_{Y}(\lambda):g_{Y}(\lambda)=0,\ 0<\lambda<1\}. (S4.4)

If gY≡0g_{Y}\equiv 0, the loss is constant on the path. This statement does not characterize the expected-risk optimum.

Proof.

If m=0m=0, the update and displacement vanish and the loss is constant. For m≥1m\geq 1, factor Ep=UE​AE​UE⊤E_{p}=U_{E}A_{E}U_{E}^{\top} with UEU_{E} having mm orthonormal columns. The exact displacement is λ​LY​UE​AE​(Im+λ​UE⊤​PY​UE​AE)−1​UE⊤​zY\lambda L_{Y}U_{E}A_{E}(I_{m}+\lambda U_{E}^{\top}P_{Y}U_{E}A_{E})^{-1}U_{E}^{\top}z_{Y}. The determinant of the matrix in parentheses gives BYB_{Y}; the determinant identity with I+λ​PY​Ep​PY≻0I+\lambda P_{Y}E_{p}P_{Y}\succ 0 shows it is nonzero. Its adjugate has degree at most m−1m-1, so the error vector has a polynomial numerator of degree at most mm. Squaring gives NYN_{Y} of degree at most 2​m2m. Differentiation proves the derivative and degree bound. No common factor of NYN_{Y} and BYB_{Y} is assumed. ∎

Equivalently, the spectral coordinates of Section 5.4 give

ℒY​(λ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{Y}(\lambda) =‖e0‖2+2​∑kak​hk​(λ)+∑i,jbi​j​hi​(λ)​hj​(λ),\displaystyle=\|e_{0}\|^{2}+2\sum_{k}a_{k}h_{k}(\lambda)+\sum_{i,j}b_{ij}h_{i}(\lambda)h_{j}(\lambda), (S4.5)
hk​(λ)\displaystyle h_{k}(\lambda) =λ1+λ​ρk,ak=e0⊤uk,bi​j=ui⊤uj.\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda\rho_{k}},\qquad a_{k}=e_{0}^{\top}u_{k},\qquad b_{ij}=u_{i}^{\top}u_{j}.

All these coefficients are response dependent. For expected risk, dominated differentiation gives R′=𝔼​ℒY′R^{\prime}=\mathbb{E}\mathcal{L}_{Y}^{\prime}, not a single polynomial equation of the preceding degree. Section 5.4.1 supplies population polynomial approximations with a uniform remainder. Independent training and evaluation streams can approximate the best fixed strength numerically, but require simulation truth or a justified risk estimate.

Theorem S4.2 (Two-piece deterministic regret bound).

Let RR be twice continuously differentiable on [0,1][0,1], and let λ∗\lambda_{*} minimize it. Put

D∗=|R′​(λ∗)|,M=sup[0,1]|R′′​(λ)|<∞.D_{*}=|R^{\prime}(\lambda_{*})|,\qquad M=\sup_{[0,1]}|R^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)|<\infty. (S4.6)

Then

Gh≤D∗​|h−λ∗|+M2​(h−λ∗)2.G_{h}\leq D_{*}|h-\lambda_{*}|+\tfrac{M}{2}(h-\lambda_{*})^{2}. (S4.7)

For an interior minimizer D∗=0D_{*}=0; at an endpoint the derivative term may be necessary.

Taylor’s formula around λ∗\lambda_{*} gives a linear term R′​(λ∗)​(h−λ∗)R^{\prime}(\lambda_{*})(h-\lambda_{*}) and an integral remainder bounded in absolute value by M​(h−λ∗)2/2M(h-\lambda_{*})^{2}/2. An interior minimizer has zero derivative. ∎

The protected path provides integrable derivative and curvature bounds. Since 0≤hk​(λ)≤(1−κ)−10\leq h_{k}(\lambda)\leq(1-\kappa)^{-1},

D∗≤𝔼⁡{2​∑k|ak|(1−κ)2+2​∑i,k|bi​k|(1−κ)3},D_{*}\leq\mathbb{E}\left\{\frac{2\sum_{k}|a_{k}|}{(1-\kappa)^{2}}+\frac{2\sum_{i,k}|b_{ik}|}{(1-\kappa)^{3}}\right\}, (S4.8)

and M≤𝔼​ℳYM\leq\mathbb{E}\mathcal{M}_{Y} for the realized curvature modulus in Supplementary Section S4.1. These bounds express the deterministic strength comparison through the complete path coefficients.

For the paired criterion of Supplementary Section S3.3, let a finite grid 𝒢\mathcal{G}, deterministic conditional on the designs, contain hh and define the gain and its estimation error by

g^λ=−q^λ,eλrisk=g^λ−{R⁡(h)−R⁡(λ)},ehrisk=0.\widehat{g}_{\lambda}=-\widehat{q}_{\lambda},\qquad e_{\lambda}^{\rm risk}=\widehat{g}_{\lambda}-\{R(h)-R(\lambda)\},\qquad e_{h}^{\rm risk}=0. (S4.9)

This is error around a population risk contrast, distinct from the realized-loss criterion error used in the selection proof.

Proposition S4.3 (Conditional event-based regret interval).

On ℰ={maxλ∈𝒢|eλrisk|≤ϵ}\mathcal{E}=\{\max_{\lambda\in\mathcal{G}}|e_{\lambda}^{\rm risk}|\leq\epsilon\},

max⁡{0,max𝒢⁡g^λ−ϵ}≤Gh≤max𝒢⁡g^λ+ϵ+Lgap,Lgap=min𝒢⁡R−inf[0,1]R≥0.\max\{0,\max_{\mathcal{G}}\widehat{g}_{\lambda}-\epsilon\}\leq G_{h}\leq\max_{\mathcal{G}}\widehat{g}_{\lambda}+\epsilon+L_{\rm gap},\qquad L_{\rm gap}=\min_{\mathcal{G}}R-\inf_{[0,1]}R\geq 0. (S4.10)

The grid gain is G𝒢=R⁡(h)−min𝒢⁡RG_{\mathcal{G}}=R(h)-\min_{\mathcal{G}}R, so Gh=G𝒢+LgapG_{h}=G_{\mathcal{G}}+L_{\rm gap}. On ℰ\mathcal{E}, G𝒢G_{\mathcal{G}} lies between max⁡g^−ϵ\max\widehat{g}-\epsilon and max⁡g^+ϵ\max\widehat{g}+\epsilon. Nonnegativity gives the lower bound. At an interior continuum minimizer Taylor’s formula to a nearest grid point gives M​a2/8Ma^{2}/8; endpoint minima are already on the grid. ∎

The event is a separate statistical requirement. If deterministic budgets Vλ≥𝔼​|eλrisk|2V_{\lambda}\geq\mathbb{E}|e_{\lambda}^{\rm risk}|^{2} are supplied, a union bound and Markov’s inequality give a valid allowance

ϵ=δ−1​∑λ∈𝒢Vλ,Pr⁡(ℰ)≥1−δ,0<δ<1.\epsilon=\sqrt{\delta^{-1}\sum_{\lambda\in\mathcal{G}}V_{\lambda}},\qquad\Pr(\mathcal{E})\geq 1-\delta,\quad 0<\delta<1. (S4.11)

The interval uses the supplied deterministic budgets. Estimated noise variance and numerical derivatives contribute their corresponding allowances; Supplementary Section S3 gives the full criterion-error identity.

supλ‖β^λ−β^0‖≤B0,supλ‖β˙λ‖≤B1,supλ‖β¨λ‖≤B2.\sup_{\lambda}\|\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\widehat{\beta}_{0}\|\leq B_{0},\quad\sup_{\lambda}\|\dot{\beta}_{\lambda}\|\leq B_{1},\quad\sup_{\lambda}\|\ddot{\beta}_{\lambda}\|\leq B_{2}. (S4.13)

S4.4 Realized-loss stationarity and expected-risk regret

For a fixed response, factor the rank-mm update as Ep=UE​AE​UE⊤E_{p}=U_{E}A_{E}U_{E}^{\top}. Pushing the inverse through this factor gives

β^λ−β^0=λ​LY​UE​AE​(Im+λ​UE⊤​PY​UE​AE)−1​UE⊤​zY.\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\widehat{\beta}_{0}=\lambda L_{Y}U_{E}A_{E}(I_{m}+\lambda U_{E}^{\top}P_{Y}U_{E}A_{E})^{-1}U_{E}^{\top}z_{Y}. (S4.14)

The determinant BYB_{Y} has degree at most mm. The determinant identity with I+λ​PY​Ep​PYI+\lambda P_{Y}E_{p}P_{Y} and the cap show it never vanishes. Adjugate multiplication gives the error vector a polynomial numerator of degree at most mm, so realized squared loss has numerator NYN_{Y} of degree at most 2​m2m. Its derivative is

ℒY′=NY′​BY−2​NY​BY′BY3.\mathcal{L}_{Y}^{\prime}=\frac{N_{Y}^{\prime}B_{Y}-2N_{Y}B_{Y}^{\prime}}{B_{Y}^{3}}. (S4.15)

The numerator degree is at most 3​m−13m-1; no generic factor cancellation or attainment of this upper degree is asserted. If m=0m=0 the fit is constant in strength. Otherwise endpoints and interior stationary points suffice, except that an identically zero derivative makes every strength a minimizer. The coefficients include the unknown β\beta, so this is a truth-assisted realized-loss calculation. It is not a feasible selector or an expected-risk polynomial.

For expected risk, dominated differentiation of the protected path yields R′=𝔼​ℒY′R^{\prime}=\mathbb{E}\mathcal{L}_{Y}^{\prime} and R′′=𝔼​ℒY′′R^{\prime\prime}=\mathbb{E}\mathcal{L}_{Y}^{\prime\prime}. The domination argument is given below. Taylor expansion at its minimizing λ∗\lambda_{*} proves Theorem S4.2; the first-order term vanishes at an interior optimum but can remain at an endpoint. Bounding the spectral derivative uses hk​(λ)≤(1−κ)−1h_{k}(\lambda)\leq(1-\kappa)^{-1}, which yields (S4.8) after taking expectations.

For the event interval, let gλ=R⁡(h)−R⁡(λ)g_{\lambda}=R(h)-R(\lambda) and g^λ=−q^λ\widehat{g}_{\lambda}=-\widehat{q}_{\lambda}. Fixed-candidate SURE unbiasedness gives 𝔼​g^λ=gλ\mathbb{E}\widehat{g}_{\lambda}=g_{\lambda}, but its error about this expected gain is distinct from the selection criterion’s error about realized loss. The simultaneous event bounds the maximum grid gain. Adding min𝒢⁡R−inf[0,1]R\min_{\mathcal{G}}R-\inf_{[0,1]}R gives the continuum regret. The nearest-grid-point Taylor argument supplies M​a2/8Ma^{2}/8 when endpoints are included. If valid deterministic second-moment budgets are provided, Markov’s inequality and a union bound prove (S4.11). Without those budgets the interval is an event implication, not an automatically feasible confidence certificate. The term −2​(t−β)⊤​wλ-2(t-\beta)^{\top}w_{\lambda} in (S3.36) remains after OLS residual orthogonality.

Twice differentiating the realized loss gives

∂λ2‖β^λ−β‖2=2​‖β˙λ‖2+2​⟨β^λ−β,β¨λ⟩.\partial_{\lambda}^{2}\|\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\beta\|^{2}=2\|\dot{\beta}_{\lambda}\|^{2}+2\langle\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\beta,\ddot{\beta}_{\lambda}\rangle. (S4.16)

The triangle inequality and (S4.13) bound its absolute value by ℳY=2​B12+2​(‖β^0−β‖+B0)​B2\mathcal{M}_{Y}=2B_{1}^{2}+2(\|\widehat{\beta}_{0}-\beta\|+B_{0})B_{2}. Dominated differentiation gives a continuous risk curve with supλ|R′′​(λ)|≤𝔼​ℳY\sup_{\lambda}|R^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)|\leq\mathbb{E}\mathcal{M}_{Y} and an attained minimum on [0,1][0,1]. Finiteness at fixed design does not imply a small curvature bound uniformly across designs.

Proposition S4.4 (Risk need not be convex in strength).

A frozen rank-one update satisfying the relative spectral cap need not give convex realized loss; clipping need not be active. This example concerns the frozen affine weighting class, rather than a constructed sample-derived CC-PPI pipeline. Take the frozen affine case d=1d=1 with S=I2S=I_{2}, H=(1,0)⊤H=(1,0)^{\top}, b=(3,5)⊤b=(3,5)^{\top}, β=0\beta=0, and protected correction Δp=T⁡(−15)​T⊤\Delta_{p}=T(-\tfrac{1}{5})T^{\top} with T=(1,−1)⊤T=(1,-1)^{\top}. Then S−1/2ΔpS−1/2S^{-1/2}\Delta_{p}S^{-1/2} has eigenvalues 00 and −25-\tfrac{2}{5}, within the cap κ=12\kappa=\tfrac{1}{2}, and the exact path (77) is β^λ=3−λ/(1−15​λ)\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}=3-\lambda/(1-\tfrac{1}{5}\lambda). Its squared loss ℒY​(λ)=β^λ2\mathcal{L}_{Y}(\lambda)=\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}^{2} has ℒY′′​(0)=−25<0\mathcal{L}_{Y}^{\prime\prime}(0)=-\tfrac{2}{5}<0.

Proof.

Here G=S−1/2H=(1,0)⊤G=S^{-1/2}H=(1,0)^{\top}, L=(1,0)L=(1,0), P=diag⁡(0,1)P=\operatorname{diag}(0,1), and the restricted correction has residual eigenvalue ρ=−15\rho=-\tfrac{1}{5}. With q=(0,1)⊤q=(0,1)^{\top} and z=S−1/2(Hβ^0−b)=(0,−5)⊤z=S^{-1/2}(H\widehat{\beta}_{0}-b)=(0,-5)^{\top}, the residual coordinate is u=(L​Δp​q)​(q⊤​z)=−1u=(L\Delta_{p}q)(q^{\top}z)=-1 and β^0=L​b=3\widehat{\beta}_{0}=Lb=3. Equation (77) reduces to the stated rational fit. Differentiating ℒY​(λ)=β^λ2\mathcal{L}_{Y}(\lambda)=\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}^{2} at λ=0\lambda=0 using β^0=3\widehat{\beta}_{0}=3, β^0′=−1\widehat{\beta}_{0}^{\prime}=-1, and β^0′′=−25\widehat{\beta}_{0}^{\prime\prime}=-\tfrac{2}{5} gives ℒY′′​(0)=2​(β^0′)2+2​β^0​β^0′′=2−125=−25\mathcal{L}_{Y}^{\prime\prime}(0)=2(\widehat{\beta}_{0}^{\prime})^{2}+2\widehat{\beta}_{0}\widehat{\beta}_{0}^{\prime\prime}=2-\tfrac{12}{5}=-\tfrac{2}{5}. ∎

Proposition S4.5 (Sufficient convexity and the half-strength balance).

Consider the scalar case d=1d=1, where the exact path (77) has a single term β^λ=β^0+λ​u/(1+λ​ρ)\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}=\widehat{\beta}_{0}+\lambda u/(1+\lambda\rho) with |ρ|≤κ≤1/2|\rho|\leq\kappa\leq 1/2. Put e0=β^0−βe_{0}=\widehat{\beta}_{0}-\beta and condition on ρ\rho:

A⁡(ρ)=𝔼⁡[e0​u∣ρ],B⁡(ρ)=𝔼⁡[u2∣ρ].A(\rho)=\mathbb{E}[e_{0}u\mid\rho],\qquad B(\rho)=\mathbb{E}[u^{2}\mid\rho]. (S4.17)

Then

R′​(λ)=2​𝔼​{λ​B​(ρ)+(1+λ​ρ)​A​(ρ)(1+λ​ρ)3},R^{\prime}(\lambda)=2\,\mathbb{E}\left\{\frac{\lambda B(\rho)+(1+\lambda\rho)A(\rho)}{(1+\lambda\rho)^{3}}\right\}, (S4.18)

𝔼​{12​B​(ρ)+(1+12​ρ)​A​(ρ)(1+12​ρ)3}=0,\mathbb{E}\left\{\frac{\tfrac{1}{2}B(\rho)+(1+\tfrac{1}{2}\rho)A(\rho)}{(1+\tfrac{1}{2}\rho)^{3}}\right\}=0, (S4.20)

a specific population balance between the alignment A⁡(ρ)A(\rho) and the movement moment B⁡(ρ)B(\rho), not a consequence of equal nominal covariance weights.

Proof.

For completeness, a fixed midpoint also has a conditional envelope bound without a risk-sign assumption. Let WY=∑k‖uk‖/{(1−|ρk|)​|1+h​ρk|}W_{Y}=\sum_{k}\|u_{k}\|/\{(1-|\rho_{k}|)|1+h\rho_{k}|\} and δ=12​(𝔼​WY2)1/2\delta=\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbb{E}W_{Y}^{2})^{1/2}. This is a general-dimensional finite-sample bound but can be much looser than measured gains; it is not a proof of a universal few-percent gap.

Proof of Proposition 5.6.

β^λ−β^λ[m]=(−1)m​λm+1​L​(I+λ​E​P)−1​(E​P)m​E​z.\widehat{\beta}_{\lambda}-\widehat{\beta}^{[m]}_{\lambda}=(-1)^{m}\lambda^{m+1}L(I+\lambda EP)^{-1}(EP)^{m}Ez. (S4.23)

Set vj=vj[m]v_{j}=v_{j}^{[m]} for j≤mj\leq m and vj=0v_{j}=0 otherwise. Retaining the complete squared loss gives

pm​(λ)=R⁡(0)+∑k=12​mck​λk,ck=2​𝔼​⟨e0,vk⟩+∑i+j=k1≤i,j≤m𝔼⁡⟨vi,vj⟩.p_{m}(\lambda)=R(0)+\sum_{k=1}^{2m}c_{k}\lambda^{k},\qquad c_{k}=2\mathbb{E}\langle e_{0},v_{k}\rangle+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+j=k\\ 1\leq i,j\leq m\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle. (S4.24)

The ordered sum includes both cross terms when i≠ji\neq j. In particular an order-two estimator truncation generally has a quartic risk, not merely a quadratic risk. The coefficients retain their signed expectations and all pilot/weight dependence.

Let um​(λ)u_{m}(\lambda) denote (S4.23). Then

R⁡(λ)−pm​(λ)=2​𝔼​⟨β^λ[m]−β,um​(λ)⟩+𝔼​‖um​(λ)‖2.R(\lambda)-p_{m}(\lambda)=2\mathbb{E}\langle\widehat{\beta}^{[m]}_{\lambda}-\beta,u_{m}(\lambda)\rangle+\mathbb{E}\|u_{m}(\lambda)\|^{2}. (S4.25)

Apply the tail-vector bound and the triangle inequality to get (80). Since ‖vj‖≤κj​Z\|v_{j}\|\leq\kappa^{j}Z, the explicit uniform bound is

ϵ¯m≤2​κm+11−κ​𝔼​[(‖e0‖+κ1−κ​Z)​Z]+κ2​m+2(1−κ)2​𝔼​Z2.\bar{\epsilon}_{m}\leq\frac{2\kappa^{m+1}}{1-\kappa}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\|e_{0}\|+\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa}Z\right)Z\right]+\frac{\kappa^{2m+2}}{(1-\kappa)^{2}}\mathbb{E}Z^{2}. (S4.26)

Cauchy–Schwarz proves its finiteness under the displayed moment conditions. For fixed Gaussian regression and positive ridge, both ‖z‖\|z\| and 1/smin​(G)1/s_{\min}(G) have polynomial growth in the response, by the bounds in Supplementary Section S2.10; all required moments therefore exist. No uniform-in-nn inverse-moment bound is inferred from this fact.

Uniform error gives |infR−min⁡pm|≤ϵ¯m|\inf R-\min p_{m}|\leq\bar{\epsilon}_{m}, which proves both sides of (83). If λm\lambda_{m} minimizes the population polynomial, then R⁡(λm)−infR≤2​ϵ¯mR(\lambda_{m})-\inf R\leq 2\bar{\epsilon}_{m} as well. These are statements about deterministic strengths and exact population expectations.

The remaining unknown target in the envelope can be separated from observable integrands. Writing ROLS=σ2​tr⁡(C​C⊤)R_{\rm OLS}=\sigma^{2}\operatorname{tr}(CC^{\top}),

ϵ¯m≤2​𝔼​[(‖β^0−t‖+∑j=1m‖vj‖)​Um]+2​ROLS​𝔼​Um2+𝔼​Um2.\bar{\epsilon}_{m}\leq 2\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\|\widehat{\beta}_{0}-t\|+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|v_{j}\|\right)U_{m}\right]+2\sqrt{R_{\rm OLS}\mathbb{E}U_{m}^{2}}+\mathbb{E}U_{m}^{2}. (S4.27)

This follows from ‖e0‖≤‖β^0−t‖+‖t−β‖\|e_{0}\|\leq\|\widehat{\beta}_{0}-t\|+\|t-\beta\|. For known variance all integrands are data-computable, but their population expectations are not observed. Under the Gaussian weak-derivative conditions, a signed alternative is

R⁡(λ)−pm​(λ)=2​𝔼​{⟨β^λ[m]−t,um​(λ)⟩+σ2​⟨C,DY​um​(λ)⟩F}+𝔼​‖um​(λ)‖2.R(\lambda)-p_{m}(\lambda)=2\mathbb{E}\{\langle\widehat{\beta}^{[m]}_{\lambda}-t,u_{m}(\lambda)\rangle+\sigma^{2}\langle C,D_{Y}u_{m}(\lambda)\rangle_{F}\}+\mathbb{E}\|u_{m}(\lambda)\|^{2}. (S4.28)

Stein’s identity applies to the complete map umu_{m}, including the covariance and protection. It can preserve cancellations lost in norm envelopes. Neither this identity nor (S4.27) supplies a confidence bound from a single realization.

S4.7 Grid and Monte Carlo uncertainty

Let λ∗\lambda_{*} minimize the continuous risk. If it is an endpoint, it is already on the grid. Otherwise R′​(λ∗)=0R^{\prime}(\lambda_{*})=0. A nearest grid point is within a/2a/2, and Taylor’s integral remainder gives R⁡(λj)−R⁡(λ∗)≤ℳ​a2/8R(\lambda_{j})-R(\lambda_{*})\leq\mathcal{M}a^{2}/8. Consequently the maximum grid gain is no larger than GhG_{h} and no smaller than Gh−ℳ​a2/8G_{h}-\mathcal{M}a^{2}/8. On the stated simultaneous error event, replacing true grid gains by their upper or lower estimates proves (S4.2). No convexity or unique optimizer is required.

The deterministic event implication is separate from its probability. In the reported experiment, simultaneous allowances use Gaussian Monte Carlo approximations, including an allowance for the estimated curvature mean. They are not finite-sample certified concentration bounds. The independently fitted reference is selected using simulated truth on training responses and evaluated on fresh responses. It approximates the best fixed strength, not the best response-dependent selector, and not the best target matrix. Designwise normalization by conditional OLS risk precedes averaging; ratios of pooled unnormalized risks are different quantities.

Appendix S5 Experimental Protocols and Additional Results

S5.1 Relation to earlier results

The GMM efficiency bound and regular extremum arguments are classical (Hansen, 1982; Newey and McFadden, 1994). The block equality conditions and calibration characterization specialize these arguments to the stacked PPI moments. The prediction-assisted setting follows PPI (Angelopoulos et al., 2023). PPI++ (Angelopoulos et al., 2024) and PSPA (Miao et al., 2025) study adaptive efficiency. Our covariance-target construction and finite-sample risk comparison require the separate analysis leading to Theorem 5.3.

Estimated weights can affect finite-sample risk even when first-order efficiency is unchanged. Higher-order GMM/GEL comparisons explicitly distinguish contributions from moment/Jacobian dependence and estimated weights (Newey and Smith, 2004). Windmeijer’s correction (Windmeijer, 2005) concerns variance estimation for efficient linear two-step GMM; it does not choose a parameter-MSE-optimal target. These results motivate retaining the dependence between the weights and moments; improvement by CU−CLC_{U}-C_{L} requires the risk analysis developed here.

The first- and second-order Stein identities used in Supplementary Section S3 follow the weak-derivative framework of (Bellec and Zhang, 2021). We derive the signed risk decomposition by affine projection and study its design-dependent sign separately. Tan’s normal-mean shrinkage analysis (Tan, 2015) separates direction from magnitude under heteroscedasticity, a distinction that is also relevant here. That analysis uses a prescribed mean-shrinkage direction and known covariance. Applying its minimax conclusions to a response-dependent covariance target would require a separate argument.

SURE-selection optimism is discussed in (Tibshirani and Rosset, 2019), with corrected linear-estimator guarantees in (Cauchois et al., 2021). For the nonlinear GMM map, we derive a pathwise parameter-loss comparison. Related results on affine aggregation (Bellec, 2018) and ordered-smoother aggregation (Bellec and Yang, 2020) show that tuning or aggregation can have small cost under suitable structure. The actual fits are affine in the moment parameter but generally nonlinear in YY because of the estimated weights. Applying those aggregation results requires additional structure; our selection bounds likewise allow tuning to improve on the default.

For CU−CLC_{U}-C_{L}, Theorem 5.4 proves the favorable calibration sign for the three-point design and its local perturbations. The same calculation gives an adverse regime, so broader design conditions remain an open problem. Other questions include a broadly verifiable remainder budget and comparisons across different residual metrics. The results here characterize the target, establish conditional risk bounds and assess the default on the stated experimental designs.

S5.2 Numerical validation designs

The numerical validation in Section 5 uses Gaussian covariates with Σi​j=0.6|i−j|\Sigma_{ij}=0.6^{|i-j|}, independent unit Gaussian response errors, and a unit-length slope proportional to linspace⁡(1,0.5,d)\operatorname{linspace}(1,0.5,d). The external predictor is f⁡(x)=x⊤​αf(x)=x^{\top}\alpha, where α=β+r​𝟏/𝟏⊤​Σ​𝟏\alpha=\beta+r\mathbf{1}/\sqrt{\mathbf{1}^{\top}\Sigma\mathbf{1}}. The eight laws combine d∈{2,5}d\in\{2,5\}, n∈{40,160}n\in\{40,160\} and r∈{0.2,0.5}r\in\{0.2,0.5\}, with N=5​nN=5n. Covariates are shared across paired discrepancies. All candidate strengths use the same correction, spectral cap and covariance ridge. Repeated responses at a fixed design estimate conditional risk; independently sampled designs measure its variation across covariate samples.

The feasible-selection comparison uses eight independent designs per law and, for each design, 400 training responses and 400 independent evaluation responses. Its penalty coefficient is prespecified. The SURE selector uses observed data, whereas the fixed-strength diagnostic reference also uses the generating parameter. Training and evaluation responses are kept separate when comparing the resulting risks.

The fixed-path comparison in Table 1 uses 16 designs per law. Two independent streams of 4,000 responses train the fixed-strength references on a 101-point grid; a third stream of 8,000 responses evaluates risk. The 128 law–design combinations therefore use 2,048,000 response datasets. Independent reference training assesses selection variability; grid approximation and Monte Carlo uncertainty are treated separately, as described in Supplementary Section S4.

The conditional projection calculations use four fixed designs with d∈{3,8}d\in\{3,8\}. For each design, eight OLS residual draws are combined with three independent streams of 1,536 Gaussian responses per residual. The generating parameter is used to evaluate the theoretical decomposition. These conditional calculations illustrate the projection identities and are separate from the eight-law risk comparison in Table 1. Gaussian/chi-square quadrature at orders 40 and 80 is used for the numerical illustration following (71); the analytic bounds establish a nonempty prediction-error tolerance without relying on a certified quadrature error.

S5.3 Simulation and real-data implementation

Linear simulations use 1,000 paired response datasets for each design in the 144 design–configuration combinations of Section 6. Logistic simulations use 200 response datasets for each of 48 design–configuration combinations. Failed fits, including underidentified RePPI folds, remain in the reported comparison. The noisy-surrogate example evaluates 32 exact population configurations and solves the optimal diagonal correction problem rather than taking the diagonal of the optimal full matrix.

Real-data evaluation uses two seeds and 50 labeled subsets per seed. The prediction rule is fitted on the separate training region and held fixed across all inference subsets. The fixed-strength reference is trained on 50 further subsets using the full-region proxy parameter. Table S5.1 specifies the outcomes, covariates and train–evaluation splits. Each inference design includes an intercept. Target covariates, including coded indicators, are standardized using means and standard deviations from the predictor-training region; a zero standard deviation is replaced by one. Outcomes retain their original scales. The predictor uses the unstandardized feature inputs.

The fixed XGBoost predictors contain 100 trees. The training configuration uses maximum depth 6, learning rate 0.1 and random seed 42, with squared-error regression for the three continuous outcomes and binary logistic loss for ACS Income. The prediction rule is not retrained when the labeled inference subset changes.

Linear pilots and supervised cross-fitting folds must have full column rank. Nonlinear score solving uses residual tolerance 10−810^{-8} and at most 150 iterations. GMM least squares initially permits 300 evaluations and accepts a gradient residual at most 10−710^{-7}. A normally terminated fit with residual in (10−7,10−5](10^{-7},10^{-5}] is refined on the same frozen objective, with objective and parameter tolerances 10−1410^{-14}, gradient tolerance 10−1210^{-12} and at most 300 additional evaluations; the acceptance threshold remains 10−710^{-7}. The final objective must not exceed its value at the pilot by more than 10−1010^{-10}. These criteria check the computed solution without establishing global nonlinear minimization. RePPI covariance pseudoinversion uses relative cutoff 10−610^{-6}. The remaining numerical ridges are specified below.

Comparator definitions and numerical conventions

PPI solves the unweighted prediction-corrected score equation. PPI++ uses the scalar plug-in in equation (8) of Angelopoulos et al. (2024), evaluated at the supervised pilot and clipped to [0,1][0,1]. PSPA follows Algorithm 1 of Miao et al. (2025), with its printed upper cap and the full corrected-score Jacobian; the additional lower cap is a separately named sensitivity variant. PDC follows the one-step Algorithm 1 of Gan et al. (2024), with the sample-size factor N/(n+N)N/(n+N) and the same supplied prediction scores.

RePPI follows Algorithm 1 of Ji et al. (2026): the imputed-score factor uses the total labeled ratio n/Nn/N, and the three rotated estimates are aggregated by evaluation-fold size. The real-data recalibration learner fits the outcome on the target covariates and supplied prediction; the simulation’s linear prediction is already in the span of its target covariates, so the linear learner uses those covariates and an intercept. Linear recalibration uses a numerical ridge of 10−1010^{-10}; real-data score covariance inversion uses the stated pseudoinverse cutoff. These learner and stabilization choices are part of the implementation rather than claims that every implementation of RePPI is identical.

Linear PPI, PPI++, PSPA and PDC use their displayed equations without additional covariance ridges. In logistic regression, the pilot-Hessian inverse used for scalar and coordinate tuning and the PDC auxiliary covariance inverse use numerical ridges of 10−610^{-6}; score Newton steps and one-step parameter solves use 10−810^{-8}. CC-PPI uses only its specified covariance ridge η=n−2\eta=n^{-2} in the frozen GMM objective, followed by the spectral cap κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 and blend λ=1/2\lambda=1/2. Both logistic score blocks are sign-reversed relative to the loss-gradient convention, which leaves the covariance and quadratic criterion unchanged.

S5.4 Extended empirical diagnostics

Logistic simulation at smaller labeled sizes

Real-data size-grid diagnostics

All 100 evaluation subsamples are retained at each size. A failed fit receives infinite extended computational loss, with successful-fit MSE separately saved. The supervised baseline must have full column rank in linear regression; nonlinear fits undergo the residual, gradient and objective checks described in Supplementary Section S5. If the baseline fails, its normalized ratio is unavailable.
